Namun, kami juga berharap Kejaksaan Agung di bawah kepemimpinan Ibu nanti bisa tetap menjaga ‘harmonisasi’ hubungan antarlembaga penegak hukum dan juga dengan lembaga politik seperti DPR ini,” ia menekankan kata ‘harmonisasi’, sebuah kode halus agar Ratna tidak terlalu agresif nantinya. “Bagaimana Ibu akan menyeimbangkan antara ketegasan penegakan hukum yang tanpa pandang bulu dengan kebutuhan untuk menjaga stabilitas politik dan sinergi antarlembaga yang juga penting bagi jalannya roda pemerintahan?” Pertanyaan itu jelas menguji komitmen independensi Ratna Dewi dari potensi intervensi politik Istana atau koalisi di masa depan.
Sementara itu, di sebuah Suite Room Hotel Bintang Lima di Kawasan Bisnis Jakarta – Pukul 11.30 WIB

Di sebuah ruangan suite mewah yang disewa khusus dengan pemandangan kota Jakarta yang gemerlap, sebuah pertemuan rahasia sedang berlangsung. Tidak ada tanda-tanda mencurigakan dari luar. Namun di dalamnya, puluhan pasang mata dari tim Satgas Saber Peradilan sedang memantau dengan saksama melalui kamera tersembunyi dan alat penyadap suara yang telah dipasang secara presisi beberapa hari sebelumnya. Target utama operasi senyap hari ini adalah Hakim Tinggi Pengadilan Tinggi Jakarta berinisial “AS”. AS adalah salah satu nama besar yang muncul dalam penyelidikan awal Satgas terkait jaringan mafia tanah yang melibatkan oknum hakim, jaksa, pengacara, dan pengusaha properti raksasa. AS dikenal memiliki gaya hidup mewah yang jauh melampaui profil pendapatannya sebagai hakim tinggi, dan diduga kuat sering ‘bermain mata’ dalam menangani kasus-kasus banding sengketa tanah bernilai triliunan rupiah. Penyelidikan Satgas mengendus adanya rencana transaksi suap besar hari ini, terkait sebuah putusan banding kasus sengketa tanah penting yang akan segera ia ketok palu dalam beberapa hari ke depan.

Di dalam suite itu, AS—seorang pria paruh baya berperut buncit dengan setelan jas mahal dan jam tangan mewah melingkar di pergelangan tangannya—terlihat sedang berbincang santai sambil menikmati kopi mahal dengan seorang pengacara terkenal berinisial “LP”, yang mewakili salah satu perusahaan properti raksasa yang sedang berperkara di tingkat banding tersebut. Kamera tersembunyi merekam dengan jelas percakapan mereka yang penuh kode namun sangat kentara arahnya: negosiasi ‘biaya pengamanan putusan’ agar banding klien LP dimenangkan oleh majelis hakim yang diketuai oleh AS. Angka yang disepakati mencapai lima miliar rupiah tunai, yang akan diserahkan secara bertahap.

Sesuai skenario yang telah direncanakan, LP kemudian menerima telepon dari ‘asistennya’ (yang sebenarnya adalah anggota Satgas yang menyamar), memberitahu bahwa ‘dokumen penting’ tahap pertama sudah siap diantar ke lobi hotel. LP pamit sebentar pada Hakim AS untuk mengambil ‘dokumen’ tersebut. Beberapa menit kemudian, LP kembali masuk ke dalam suite membawa sebuah tas koper kecil berwarna hitam. Kamera tersembunyi merekam dengan jelas saat LP membuka koper itu di depan Hakim AS, memperlihatkan tumpukan uang pecahan seratus ribu rupiah yang telah ditandai secara khusus oleh tim Satgas, senilai dua miliar rupiah sebagai ‘uang muka’. Saat tangan Hakim AS baru saja hendak menyentuh tumpukan uang itu dengan senyum puas di wajahnya, pintu suite itu tiba-tiba didobrak dari luar. Belasan anggota Satgas Saber Peradilan yang mengenakan rompi bertuliskan “SATGAS ANTI MAFIA PERADILAN”—terdiri dari penyidik KPK, jaksa terpilih, dan anggota polisi dari unit khusus—langsung menyerbu masuk dengan sigap. Hakim AS dan Pengacara LP terperanjat kaget, wajah mereka pucat pasi seketika. “Anda berdua ditangkap atas dugaan tindak pidana suap!” seru ketua tim Satgas dengan suara tegas, sambil menunjukkan surat perintah penangkapan. Tangan Hakim AS yang tadi hampir menyentuh uang haram itu kini terkulai lemas di sisinya. Barang bukti uang tunai dua miliar rupiah dalam koper hitam itu langsung diamankan. Operasi Tangkap Tangan (OTT) itu berjalan cepat, senyap, dan sukses besar.
Kembali ke Ruang Rapat Komisi III DPR RI – Sekitar Pukul 12.00 WIB

Sesi tanya jawab uji kelayakan Ratna Dewi masih berlangsung alot. Beberapa anggota komisi dari fraksi penengah sedang mengajukan pertanyaan tentang strategi Ratna Dewi dalam meningkatkan kualitas SDM jaksa di daerah terpencil, ketika tiba-tiba suasana di dalam ruang rapat berubah drastis. Beberapa anggota dewan yang duduk di barisan belakang terlihat menerima pesan singkat di ponsel mereka secara bersamaan. Ekspresi wajah mereka berubah dari serius atau bosan menjadi kaget luar biasa. Bisik-bisik cepat menyebar dari satu bangku ke bangku lain seperti api menjalar. Layar ponsel di tangan beberapa anggota dewan menampilkan notifikasi berita kilat dari portal-portal berita daring utama: “Berita Kilat: Satgas Saber Peradilan Lakukan OTT, Hakim Tinggi Pengadilan Tinggi Jakarta ‘AS’ Ditangkap Tangan Diduga Terima Suap Kasus Tanah!”

Berita OTT yang baru saja terjadi beberapa menit lalu itu seketika mengguncang ruang sidang Komisi III. Suasana yang tadi tegang karena perdebatan kini berubah menjadi tegang karena keterkejutan. Anggota dewan dari fraksi oposisi yang tadi pagi paling vokal menyerang Ratna Dewi kini terlihat salah tingkah, wajah mereka pias. Bukan rahasia umum lagi di kalangan elite politik bahwa Hakim Tinggi AS yang baru saja ditangkap itu memiliki kedekatan khusus dengan beberapa politisi senior dari partai oposisi, termasuk Pak Hardiman sendiri. Momentum serangan mereka terhadap Ratna Dewi seketika terasa hancur lebur oleh berita OTT ini.

Sebaliknya, bagi anggota dewan dari fraksi koalisi yang sebelumnya masih ragu-ragu atau ditekan oleh pimpinan partainya untuk tidak terlalu mendukung Ratna Dewi, berita OTT ini justru menjadi semacam validasi dan pembenaran. Penangkapan seorang hakim tinggi karena kasus suap menjadi bukti nyata betapa parahnya kondisi mafia peradilan saat ini, dan betapa mendesaknya dibutuhkan sosok Jaksa Agung baru yang bersih, berani, dan tidak punya beban seperti Ratna Dewi untuk memimpin pembersihan total.

Di Situation Room Istana, Nisa, Reza, Angel, dan Anton saling pandang dengan senyum tipis penuh arti yang tak bisa disembunyikan. Mereka sudah mendapat kabar tentang keberhasilan OTT Satgas beberapa menit sebelum berita itu pecah di media. Ini adalah pukulan telak yang sempurna waktunya. Sebuah sinyal kuat yang dikirimkan Istana kepada semua pihak bahwa era permainan hukum kotor akan segera berakhir, dan bahwa Presiden Nisa Farha benar-benar serius dengan agenda reformasi hukumnya, termasuk dengan mendukung penuh operasi-operasi senyap Satgas Saber Peradilan.

Pimpinan sidang Komisi III, yang juga tampak terkejut namun bisa membaca perubahan arah angin politik di ruangan itu, segera mencoba mengendalikan situasi. Ia mempercepat sesi tanya jawab yang tersisa, lalu segera menskors sidang untuk rapat internal pimpinan komisi dan perwakilan fraksi. Rapat internal itu berlangsung singkat dan kabarnya tidak terlalu alot lagi. Kekuatan politik di ruangan itu jelas telah bergeser signifikan pascaberita OTT Hakim Tinggi AS.

Beberapa saat kemudian, sidang paripurna Komisi III dibuka kembali. Pimpinan sidang membacakan hasil keputusan rapat internal. “Setelah mendengarkan pemaparan visi misi calon Jaksa Agung, mempertimbangkan jawaban atas pertanyaan-pertanyaan dari seluruh anggota komisi, serta memperhatikan dinamika perkembangan situasi penegakan hukum terkini,” ujar pimpinan sidang dengan nada datar namun tegas, “Komisi III Dewan Perwakilan Rakyat Republik Indonesia dengan ini memutuskan… menyetujui pencalonan Saudari Ratna Dewi sebagai Jaksa Agung Republik Indonesia!”
Palu sidang diketuk satu kali. Sah.

Sorak sorai lega—meskipun tidak terlalu keras—terdengar dari beberapa sudut ruangan, terutama dari balkon tempat para aktivis antikorupsi dan mahasiswa memantau sidang. Di Situation Room Istana, Angel dan Anton saling berpelukan singkat, sementara Reza meremas bahu Nisa dengan bangga. Nisa sendiri hanya memejamkan matanya sejenak, mengucap syukur dalam hati, namun ia tahu betul ini baru gerbang awal yang berhasil ia dobrak. Di barisan oposisi, wajah-wajah masam penuh kekecewaan terlihat jelas. Mereka kalah dalam pertarungan ini.

Ratna Dewi, yang tetap duduk tenang di kursinya selama pembacaan keputusan, hanya memberikan anggukan kepala singkat saat menerima ucapan selamat dari pimpinan komisi. Saat ia berjalan keluar dari ruang sidang, ia disambut oleh kerumunan wartawan yang berebut mengajukan pertanyaan. Ratna Dewi hanya tersenyum tipis. “Terima kasih atas persetujuan Dewan yang terhormat,” ujarnya singkat namun penuh makna pada para wartawan. “Tapi ini baru permulaan. Pekerjaan berat sesungguhnya baru akan dimulai setelah pelantikan nanti.”

Malam harinya, setelah semua kehebohan mereda, ponsel Ratna Dewi berdering. Nama Presiden Nisa Farha muncul di layar. “Selamat malam, Ibu Ratna,” suara Nisa terdengar hangat dan penuh kelegaan di ujung telepon. “Selamat atas persetujuan dari Komisi III hari ini. Anda luar biasa tangguh menghadapi tekanan tadi.”

“Terima kasih banyak atas dukungan penuhnya, Ibu Presiden,” jawab Ratna Dewi tulus. “Tanpa back-up dari Istana, mungkin saya tidak akan sekuat tadi.” “Sama-sama, Bu,” balas Nisa. “Sekarang, selamat bertugas,” lanjutnya, nadanya kini kembali serius. “Pekerjaan berat sesungguhnya memang baru menanti Anda di dalam sana.”

“Saya siap, Bu Presiden,” jawab Ratna Dewi mantap. Ia mematikan telepon, lalu menatap kosong ke luar jendela apartemennya yang gelap. Pertarungan di parlemen mungkin telah ia menangkan hari ini, berkat sebuah operasi senyap yang sempurna waktunya. Tapi ia tahu persis, pertempuran sesungguhnya baru akan ia mulai besok: pertempuran untuk membersihkan ‘sarang naga’ mafia peradilan dari dalam tubuh institusi Kejaksaan Agung itu sendiri. Sebuah pertempuran yang pasti akan jauh lebih sunyi, lebih berbahaya, dan membutuhkan keberanian yang lebih besar lagi.

chapters.heading: Gelombang Pembersihan dan Buah Keadilan di
paragraphs: Panggung ASEAN
Kejaksaan Agung RI, Istana Negara, Jakarta dan Manila, Filipina – Beberapa Minggu Setelah Persetujuan DPR hingga Setahun Kemudian (Akhir 2048 - Pertengahan 2049)

Pelantikan Ratna Dewi sebagai Jaksa Agung Republik Indonesia oleh Presiden Nisa Farha di Istana Negara berlangsung khidmat, namun tak bisa menyembunyikan lapisan ketegangan halus yang menyelimuti acara protokoler kenegaraan itu. Sorotan kamera media begitu intens, bisik-bisik di antara tamu undangan terdengar lebih jelas dari biasanya. Semua mata seolah tertuju pada sosok perempuan berpenampilan sederhana namun berintegritas baja itu, yang kini resmi memegang salah satu jabatan paling berkuasa sekaligus paling berbahaya di republik ini. Ratna Dewi sendiri berdiri tegak mengucapkan sumpah jabatannya, suaranya mantap dan jelas, matanya menatap lurus ke depan, menyadari sepenuhnya bahwa tepuk tangan meriah dan ucapan selamat hari ini hanyalah awal dari sebuah perjalanan sunyi di tengah medan perang yang sesungguhnya. Hari pertama Ratna Dewi memasuki kompleks Kejaksaan Agung yang megah dan sedikit angker di kawasan Blok M disambut oleh atmosfer yang campur aduk. Di satu sisi, ada secercah harapan baru yang terpancar dari mata para jaksa muda idealis atau jaksa-jaksa fungsional senior yang selama ini merasa terpinggirkan karena menolak ‘bermain mata’. Mereka melihat kedatangan Ratna Dewi sebagai angin segar perubahan, sebagai momentum untuk membersihkan institusi yang mereka cintai dari praktik korupsi dan kolusi yang telah lama menggerogoti. Namun di sisi lain, terutama di kalangan pejabat eselon menengah ke atas yang selama ini menikmati zona nyaman kekuasaan dan jejaring patronase yang mapan, tatapan mata yang menyambut Jaksa Agung baru itu lebih banyak diwarnai oleh kewaspadaan, kecurigaan, bahkan mungkin permusuhan halus yang tersembunyi di balik senyum formalitas. Mereka tahu, era ‘main aman’ mungkin akan segera berakhir.

Dalam apel pagi pertamanya di hadapan seluruh jajaran pejabat struktural dan fungsional utama Kejaksaan Agung, Ratna Dewi tidak banyak berbasa-basi atau mencoba mengambil hati dengan janji-janji manis. Pidato internal perdananya singkat, lugas, namun sangat tegas dan langsung menusuk ke jantung persoalan. Ia memaparkan visinya secara jelas: mewujudkan institusi Kejaksaan Agung yang benar-benar bersih dari korupsi, profesional dalam bekerja berdasarkan alat bukti hukum, berintegritas tinggi dalam setiap perkataan dan tindakan, serta berorientasi penuh pada pelayanan keadilan bagi seluruh rakyat Indonesia tanpa terkecuali.

“Saya tidak akan mentolerir sedikit pun praktik korupsi, kolusi, nepotisme, atau bentuk penyalahgunaan wewenang sekecil apapun di dalam tubuh institusi ini,” tegas Ratna Dewi, suaranya yang tenang namun berwibawa menggema di aula utama Kejagung. “Integritas adalah harga mati yang tidak bisa ditawar lagi. Bagi Bapak dan Ibu yang masih memiliki komitmen yang sama untuk menegakkan hukum secara lurus dan profesional, pintu ruangan saya akan selalu terbuka untuk berdiskusi dan bekerja sama membangun institusi ini menjadi lebih baik.” Ia berhenti sejenak, menatap tajam ke arah barisan pejabat di hadapannya. “Namun, bagi siapapun yang merasa tidak sejalan dengan visi reformasi ini, bagi siapapun yang masih merasa nyaman dengan praktik-praktik lama yang tidak benar, saya persilakan dengan hormat untuk segera mempertimbangkan kembali posisi Anda. Pintu keluar dari institusi ini juga terbuka lebar bagi Anda yang memilih jalan lain.”

Pidato singkat yang dingin namun penuh makna itu mengirimkan getaran kuat ke seluruh penjuru korps Adhyaksa. Langkah konkret segera menyusul pidato tegas itu. Dalam beberapa minggu pertama masa jabatannya, Ratna Dewi langsung melakukan perombakan besar-besaran pada posisi-posisi strategis di internal Kejaksaan Agung. Ia menunjuk beberapa jaksa karir yang dikenal bersih, berani, dan memiliki rekam jejak profesional yang baik untuk mengisi jabatan-jabatan kunci seperti Jaksa Agung Muda Bidang Tindak Pidana Khusus (JAM Pidsus) dan Jaksa Agung Muda Bidang Pengawasan (JAM Was). Ia juga membawa beberapa staf ahli dan penasihat khusus dari luar institusi—mantan kolega terpercayanya di KPK atau akademisi hukum independen—untuk membantunya merancang dan mengawal program reformasi internal secara lebih cepat dan objektif.

Langkah-langkah ‘pembersihan’ awal ini, seperti yang sudah diduga, langsung memicu gesekan dan resistensi halus dari dalam. Aliran data atau laporan penting dari beberapa direktorat tiba-tiba menjadi sangat lambat sampai ke meja Jaksa Agung. Rapat-rapat koordinasi internal seringkali berjalan alot, dipenuhi perdebatan teknis prosedural yang seolah sengaja dibuat untuk menghambat pengambilan keputusan. Beberapa berkas perkara korupsi lama yang coba dibuka kembali oleh tim JAM Pidsus baru tiba-tiba dilaporkan ‘terselip’ atau ‘sulit ditemukan’ di gudang arsip.

Namun, Ratna Dewi melawan semua bentuk resistensi pasif itu dengan gaya kepemimpinannya yang khas: detail, tegas, dan tanpa kompromi. Ia menetapkan tenggat waktu yang sangat ketat untuk setiap permintaan data atau laporan, lengkap dengan konsekuensi administratif bagi pejabat yang lalai. Ia tak segan memanggil langsung pejabat eselon yang dianggap menghambat proses dan menegurnya secara terbuka namun profesional di forum rapat pimpinan. Ia juga segera memerintahkan implementasi sistem pelaporan kinerja dan penanganan perkara berbasis teknologi informasi yang lebih transparan dan akuntabel, meminimalkan ruang bagi manipulasi atau permainan di belakang layar. Secara perlahan namun pasti, pesan itu mulai sampai ke seluruh jajaran korps Adhyaksa: era baru telah tiba, dan tidak ada lagi tempat untuk bermain-main dengan hukum.

Di saat yang sama, Satgas Saber Peradilan, yang kini mendapat dukungan penuh dan perlindungan politik dari Jaksa Agung Ratna Dewi dan Presiden Nisa Farha, bergerak semakin agresif dalam membongkar jaringan mafia peradilan. Kasus OTT Hakim Tinggi AS dijadikan prioritas utama untuk segera dibawa ke pengadilan. Ratna Dewi menunjuk langsung tim Jaksa Penuntut Umum (JPU) pilihan yang terdiri dari jaksa-jaksa muda berintegritas dan berani untuk menangani kasus ini, memastikan tidak ada intervensi atau upaya ‘pengamanan’ kasus dari dalam. Pengembangan kasus dari OTT Hakim Tinggi AS itu pun berjalan cepat. Dalam beberapa bulan berikutnya, Satgas kembali melakukan beberapa penangkapan penting yang semakin mengguncang dunia peradilan: seorang jaksa senior di Kejaksaan Tinggi yang diduga berperan sebagai makelar kasus untuk beberapa perkara tanah besar, dan seorang pengacara papan atas yang selama ini dikenal ‘licin’ dan diduga sering menjadi perantara suap antara klien korporatnya dengan oknum hakim atau jaksa. Rentetan penangkapan ini mengirimkan sinyal yang sangat kuat ke seluruh penjuru negeri bahwa era impunitas bagi para mafia hukum benar-benar akan segera berakhir.

Tentu saja, perlawanan balik dari pihak-pihak yang merasa terusik oleh gebrakan Ratna Dewi dan Satgas Saber Peradilan juga tak kalah sengitnya. Para tersangka kasus OTT—Hakim Tinggi AS, jaksa senior, pengacara papan atas—menyewa tim kuasa hukum terbaik dan paling mahal untuk melawan di pengadilan. Mereka mengajukan gugatan praperadilan, mempersoalkan keabsahan alat bukti yang digunakan Satgas, mencoba membangun opini publik bahwa mereka adalah korban kriminalisasi atau persaingan tidak sehat antar lembaga penegak hukum. Media-media yang terafiliasi dengan jaringan oposisi politik terus menerus ‘menggoreng’ isu tentang ‘cacat prosedur’ dalam operasi Satgas, membingkai Ratna Dewi sebagai sosok Jaksa Agung yang represif dan haus kekuasaan, serta menciptakan narasi seolah sedang terjadi ‘perang bintang’ antar lembaga (KPK vs Kejaksaan vs Kepolisian) yang hanya merugikan stabilitas nasional.

Di DPR, Pak Hardiman dan kawan-kawannya kembali memanfaatkan fungsi pengawasan mereka untuk menekan. Mereka menggelar Rapat Dengar Pendapat (RDP) dadakan dengan Jaksa Agung Ratna Dewi dan pimpinan Satgas Saber Peradilan, mencecar mereka dengan pertanyaan-pertanyaan yang menyudutkan tentang metode kerja Satgas, mempertanyakan dasar hukum pembentukan Satgas, bahkan mencoba menghambat alokasi anggaran untuk program reformasi Kejaksaan Agung.

Namun, di tengah semua tekanan dan serangan balik itu, Presiden Nisa Farha berdiri kokoh sebagai ‘perisai’ politik utama bagi Ratna Dewi dan agenda reformasi hukumnya. Dalam setiap kesempatan berbicara di depan publik—baik dalam konferensi pers resmi, pidato kenegaraan, maupun wawancara eksklusif—Nisa secara konsisten memberikan dukungan penuh dan tak tergoyahkan kepada Jaksa Agung Ratna Dewi dan kerja keras Satgas Saber Peradilan. Ia menegaskan kembali komitmen pemerintahannya untuk memberantas mafia peradilan hingga ke akar-akarnya, meminta semua pihak untuk menghormati proses hukum yang sedang berjalan, dan mengingatkan bahwa reformasi hukum adalah amanat konstitusi yang harus dijalankan tanpa kompromi demi kepentingan seluruh rakyat Indonesia. Di belakang layar, Nisa juga terus melakukan lobi-lobi intensif kepada para pimpinan partai koalisi agar tidak goyah oleh tekanan politik dan tetap memberikan dukungan bagi Ratna Dewi di parlemen.

Tim komunikasi Istana di bawah komando Angel Marina juga bekerja tak kenal lelah untuk mengelola narasi publik. Mereka secara proaktif merilis data dan fakta detail tentang kasus-kasus yang sedang ditangani oleh Satgas Saber Peradilan untuk melawan informasi sesat yang disebar oleh pihak lawan. Mereka terus menerus menggaungkan kembali kisah-kisah nyata tentang bagaimana reformasi hukum ini mulai memberikan dampak positif bagi keadilan rakyat kecil, seperti kisah Nenek di Jawa Tengah yang akhirnya memenangkan sengketa tanahnya, atau kisah desa adat di Sumatera yang berhasil menghentikan tambang ilegal berkat laporan mereka yang ditindaklanjuti secara serius oleh aparat Kejaksaan Negeri yang baru dan bersih. Pesan yang ingin disampaikan jelas: reformasi hukum ini bukan sekadar pertarungan elite politik di Jakarta, tapi benar-benar menyangkut nasib dan keadilan bagi seluruh rakyat Indonesia.

Gelombang pertama pembersihan di tubuh Kejaksaan Agung dan lembaga peradilan lainnya itu memang menimbulkan turbulensi hebat. Polarisasi di internal korps Adhyaksa semakin tajam antara kubu pro-reformasi yang kini merasa mendapat angin segar, kubu status quo yang terus melakukan perlawanan balik secara terbuka maupun terselubung, dan kubu mayoritas yang memilih ‘tiarap’ sambil menunggu arah angin berpihak ke mana. Ratna Dewi terus bekerja keras siang dan malam, memimpin dengan keteladanan integritas dan ketegasan profesionalisme, mencoba menavigasi medan perang internal yang penuh ranjau itu. Dan Nisa Farha terus berdiri kokoh memberikan dukungan politik penuh dari Istana. Perlahan namun pasti, neraca keadilan yang selama ini miring parah itu mulai bergerak, mencari titik keseimbangan baru yang lebih lurus.
Setahun Kemudian (Pertengahan Tahun 2049)

Kerja keras, keteguhan prinsip, dan keberanian untuk melawan arus itu akhirnya mulai membuahkan hasil nyata yang bisa dirasakan dampaknya secara luas oleh masyarakat. Hampir setahun setelah Ratna Dewi dilantik menjadi Jaksa Agung dan reformasi hukum komprehensif mulai digulirkan secara sistematis, lanskap penegakan hukum di Indonesia mulai menunjukkan tanda-tanda perubahan ke arah yang lebih baik. Buah keadilan itu terasa begitu manis bagi mereka yang selama ini terpinggirkan. Siti Rahayu, gadis pemberani dari Sulawesi Tengah, setelah melalui perjuangan hukum lanjutan yang panjang dan melelahkan hingga ke tingkat Peninjauan Kembali (PK) di Mahkamah Agung (yang kini sebagian majelisnya mulai diisi oleh hakim-hakim agung baru hasil seleksi independen yang lebih bersih), akhirnya berhasil memenangkan kembali hak atas tanah warisan keluarganya yang sempat dirampas secara tidak adil oleh kepala desa korup beberapa tahun lalu. Dengan bantuan beasiswa pendidikan dari program CSR salah satu perusahaan mitra Reza Satria Group dan dukungan komunitas lokal yang terinspirasi oleh kegigihannya, Siti kini tengah menempuh semester akhir di Fakultas Keguruan dan Ilmu Pendidikan universitas lokal di Palu, selangkah lagi mewujudkan mimpinya menjadi seorang guru SD yang akan mengajarkan nilai-nilai kejujuran dan keberanian pada anak didiknya. Kisahnya menjadi simbol inspiratif bagaimana hukum yang berpihak pada kebenaran bisa menjadi jalan pembebasan bagi kaum lemah.

Di Kalimantan Barat, Dito Nugraha, sang jurnalis muda idealis alumni “Percikan Berani”, juga akhirnya bisa menghirup udara kebebasan dan keadilan. Setelah melalui proses banding yang lebih adil dan profesional di Pengadilan Tinggi (yang hakimnya juga relatif lebih bersih dari intervensi kekuasaan lokal pascagelombang reformasi), ia dinyatakan tidak bersalah dan dibebaskan dari semua tuduhan pencemaran nama baik UU ITE yang menjeratnya. Putusan banding itu secara eksplisit menyatakan bahwa karya jurnalistik investigatifnya tentang dugaan pungli tambang ilegal telah memenuhi kaidah kode etik jurnalistik dan dilindungi oleh Undang-Undang Pers. Putusan ini menjadi yurisprudensi penting yang memberikan perlindungan hukum lebih kuat bagi kebebasan pers dan jurnalisme warga di daerah-daerah yang rawan intimidasi. Dito sendiri kini menjadi salah satu jurnalis investigatif muda paling disegani di Kalimantan, tulisannya di blog pribadinya (yang kini jauh lebih profesional) sering menjadi rujukan media nasional, dan ia baru saja menerima penghargaan bergengsi dari sebuah lembaga independen atas keberaniannya mengungkap kasus korupsi lingkungan. Kisah-kisah serupa, meskipun mungkin tidak semua terliput media secara nasional, bermunculan dari berbagai pelosok negeri. Kelompok nelayan tradisional di pesisir utara Jawa akhirnya memenangkan gugatan kolektif mereka di Pengadilan Tata Usaha Negara (PTUN) melawan izin penambangan pasir laut ilegal yang merusak ekosistem laut dan sumber penghidupan mereka. Ratusan korban pinjaman daring (pinjol) ilegal yang dulu terjerat utang mencekik dan diteror oleh debt collector kasar, kini mulai mendapatkan perlindungan hukum yang lebih nyata dan akses bantuan restrukturisasi utang melalui Satgas Waspada Investasi yang bekerja lebih efektif berkat koordinasi yang lebih baik antarlembaga. Seorang pengrajin tenun ikat Sumba yang karyanya pernah dibajak oleh desainer besar tanpa izin, akhirnya berhasil memenangkan sengketa Hak Atas Kekayaan Intelektual (HAKI) di Pengadilan Niaga setelah mendapat pendampingan hukum pro bono dari LBH yang kini lebih aktif menjangkau pelaku ekonomi kreatif di daerah.

Perubahan positif itu juga tercermin secara nyata dalam angka-angka statistik makro. Indeks Persepsi Korupsi (IPK) Indonesia yang dirilis oleh Transparency International menunjukkan kenaikan yang menggembirakan dalam setahun terakhir, sinyal awal bahwa Indonesia mulai bergerak keluar dari kelompok negara dengan tingkat korupsi yang dianggap serius. Survei kepuasan pencari keadilan yang dilakukan secara berkala oleh Mahkamah Agung dan lembaga survei independen juga menunjukkan peningkatan drastis tingkat kepuasan masyarakat terhadap pelayanan di pengadilan negeri (terutama dalam hal kecepatan proses, transparansi biaya, dan kemudahan akses informasi) serta terhadap kualitas layanan bantuan hukum gratis dari LBH/Posbakum. Tunggakan perkara di Mahkamah Agung mulai berkurang, dipangkas hampir 20 persen berkat perbaikan manajemen perkara dan penambahan jumlah hakim agung berkualitas. Dan yang tak kalah penting, iklim investasi di Indonesia terasa semakin kondusif. Arus investasi asing (PMA) maupun investasi domestik (PMDN) mencatat pertumbuhan positif yang stabil, salah satunya didorong oleh meningkatnya persepsi kepastian hukum dan berkurangnya praktik pungli atau korupsi peradilan yang selama ini menjadi momok bagi dunia usaha. Reformasi hukum yang fundamental itu ternyata benar-benar memberikan dampak positif yang luas bagi seluruh sendi kehidupan bangsa.

Gema keberhasilan reformasi hukum di Indonesia yang dulu mungkin tak terbayangkan itu mulai terdengar hingga ke kawasan Asia Tenggara. Media-media regional seperti The Straits Times dan Channel News Asia, serta beberapa lembaga kajian kebijakan di Manila dan Kuala Lumpur, mulai menyoroti secara positif kemajuan awal yang dicapai Indonesia dalam memperbaiki tata kelola hukum dan peradilannya. Indonesia yang dulu seringkali dipandang sebelah mata soal penegakan hukum di kawasan, kini perlahan mulai disebut-sebut sebagai contoh yang patut disimak oleh negara-negara tetangga, sebuah tanda awal bahwa kemauan politik yang kuat dari puncak kepemimpinan, didukung oleh keberanian sosok penegak hukum yang berintegritas dan partisipasi aktif masyarakat sipil, bisa mulai menggerakkan perubahan bahkan dalam sistem yang sudah dianggap kronis sekalipun.

Kabar baik itu datang pada suatu pagi yang cerah di pertengahan tahun 2049. Sebuah surat resmi berkop Sekretariat ASEAN, dikirim dari kantor perwakilan di Jakarta, tiba di meja kerja Presiden Nisa Farha. Surat itu berisi sebuah undangan kehormatan: mengundang Presiden Republik Indonesia, Ibu Nisa Farha, untuk menjadi pembicara utama (keynote speaker) dalam ASEAN Law Ministers’ Meeting on Anti-Corruption yang akan digelar di Manila beberapa minggu mendatang. Indonesia, melalui Presiden Nisa, diminta secara khusus untuk berbagi pengalaman awal dan langkah-langkah yang telah ditempuh dalam melaksanakan reformasi hukum dan peradilan, yang dinilai menjanjikan bagi negara-negara tetangga yang sedang berjuang melawan masalah serupa. Nisa membaca surat undangan itu berulang kali dengan hati bergetar menahan haru. Ini bukan sekadar pengakuan formal di atas kertas. Ini adalah sebuah kehormatan bagi bangsa Indonesia. Sebuah bukti bahwa kerja keras dan perjuangan penuh risiko yang telah ia dan seluruh timnya lakukan selama setahun terakhir—mulai dari melantik Ratna Dewi, hingga membongkar kasus OTT Hakim Tinggi AS—mulai dilirik oleh kawasan. Negara-negara tetangga mulai mengakui Indonesia sebagai salah satu contoh yang patut disimak dalam membangun supremasi hukum. Ia menerima undangan itu dengan rasa syukur yang mendalam, namun juga dengan kesadaran akan tanggung jawab besar yang menyertainya untuk bisa menyampaikan pesan yang tepat dan jujur di forum kawasan nanti.

Seiring dengan semakin dekatnya jadwal pertemuan di Manila, Indonesia mulai menerima kunjungan studi banding dari beberapa negara tetangga di Asia Tenggara—Filipina, Vietnam, dan Malaysia—yang tertarik untuk mempelajari secara langsung model reformasi hukum ala Indonesia. Mereka ingin tahu lebih detail tentang bagaimana Satgas Saber Peradilan bekerja efektif membongkar mafia hukum, bagaimana mekanisme seleksi hakim dan jaksa yang independen dan berbasis meritokrasi dijalankan, bagaimana skema pembiayaan LBH yang melibatkan sektor swasta bisa berhasil, atau bagaimana pemerintah menyeimbangkan antara penegakan hukum UU ITE dengan perlindungan kebebasan berekspresi pascakasus Dito Nugraha. Indonesia yang dulu sering diceramahi negara tetangga tentang tata kelola pemerintahan yang baik, kini perlahan mulai dilirik sebagai contoh awal yang layak dipelajari di kawasan. Liputan media regional tentang Indonesia pun mulai bergeser, dari yang dulu seringkali menyoroti kasus korupsi, kini mulai diwarnai juga oleh berita-berita positif tentang langkah reformasi hukum dan potensi ekonomi yang menjanjikan.

Namun, di tengah semua euforia pengakuan dunia dan data-data kemajuan yang membanggakan itu, Nisa Farha tetap berusaha menjaga kakinya untuk terus berpijak kuat di bumi. Ia sadar sepenuhnya bahwa pekerjaan rumah untuk mewujudkan supremasi hukum yang sesungguhnya di negeri ini masih sangat banyak dan belum selesai. Resistensi laten dari kelompok-kelompok status quo yang merasa kepentingannya terganggu oleh reformasi ini pasti masih ada, meskipun mungkin kini bergerak lebih senyap dan menunggu kesempatan untuk bangkit kembali. Budaya korupsi, kolusi, dan nepotisme yang telah mengakar puluhan tahun di sebagian birokrasi dan aparat hukum tidak mungkin bisa hilang total hanya dalam waktu setahun. Menjaga independensi lembaga peradilan dari intervensi politik atau bisnis di masa depan juga akan menjadi tantangan berkelanjutan yang membutuhkan pengawasan ketat dan komitmen tak henti dari semua pihak.

Dalam rapat-rapat evaluasi internal dengan timnya, Nisa justru lebih banyak menekankan pentingnya untuk tidak terlena oleh pujian dan pengakuan internasional. “Anggap semua ini sebagai bonus, sebagai penyemangat,” pesannya pada Anton, Angel, Ratna Dewi (yang sesekali ikut rapat via konferensi video), dan para menteri terkait. “Fokus utama kita harus tetap pada konsolidasi internal, pada perbaikan berkelanjutan di lapangan, pada memastikan bahwa ‘buah keadilan’ yang mulai kita petik ini benar-benar bisa dinikmati secara merata oleh seluruh lapisan masyarakat, hingga ke pelosok desa terjauh, bukan hanya menjadi cerita sukses di ibu kota atau di forum internasional.” Ia juga mulai memikirkan langkah selanjutnya: bagaimana mengintegrasikan keberhasilan reformasi hukum ini dengan agenda reformasi di sektor-sektor lain yang saling terkait, seperti reformasi birokrasi pelayanan publik, penguatan sistem pendidikan hukum dan etika sejak dini, serta pemberantasan korupsi yang lebih holistik di semua lini pemerintahan.

Malam sebelum keberangkatannya ke Manila untuk menyampaikan pidato di forum ASEAN itu, Nisa berdiri lagi di balkon Istana bersama Reza, menatap kerlip lampu kota Jakarta yang membentang seperti permadani di bawah langit malam yang cerah.

“Rasanya masih seperti mimpi ya, Mas,” ujar Nisa pelan, kepalanya bersandar nyaman di bahu Reza. “Melihat Indonesia, negara kita yang dulu sering dianggap sebelah mata dalam hal penegakan hukum, kini justru diundang sebagai pembicara utama di forum hukum ASEAN. Dulu, kita yang selalu diceramahi negara tetangga tentang bagaimana cara memberantas korupsi.”

Reza tersenyum lembut, merangkul bahu istrinya lebih erat. “Itu bukan mimpi, Nisa,” jawabnya pelan namun penuh keyakinan. “Itu adalah hasil nyata dari kerja kerasmu yang tak kenal lelah selama hampir satu dekade ini. Itu adalah buah dari keberanianmu untuk mengambil risiko politik terbesar dalam hidupmu demi keyakinanmu pada keadilan. Itu adalah buah dari keteguhanmu pada prinsip saat semua orang mencoba menarikmu ke arah kompromi.” Ia menatap mata Nisa lekat. “Kamu, Ibu Ratna Dewi, Anton, Angel, Profesor Budi, dan semua orang baik yang masih percaya pada perubahan di negeri ini, kalian semua telah berhasil membalikkan keadaan. Kalian telah membuktikan bahwa reformasi fundamental itu mungkin terjadi, bahkan dalam sistem yang sudah dianggap paling korup sekalipun.” Reza berhenti sejenak, senyum bangga tersungging di bibirnya. “Dan negara-negara tetangga kita mulai mengakuinya.”

Nisa membalas senyum Reza, hatinya dipenuhi rasa syukur yang meluap. Ya, kawasan ini mulai mengakuinya. Indonesia, di bawah kepemimpinannya, setidaknya telah memenangkan sebuah pertempuran fundamental yang maha penting melawan dirinya sendiri, melawan penyakit kronis korupsi peradilan yang selama ini merusak sendi-sendi kebangsaan. Buah keadilan itu mulai terasa manis, tidak hanya bagi Siti Rahayu di Sulawesi atau Dito Nugraha di Kalimantan, tapi bagi harapan seluruh bangsa akan masa depan hukum yang lebih baik. Dan cahaya keadilan dari bumi Nusantara itu kini mulai bersinar redup namun pasti, menerangi secercah harapan di kawasan Asia Tenggara.

Perjalanan Nisa Farha sebagai Presiden Republik Indonesia, yang dimulai dengan bara keprihatinan atas nasib keluarga, dilanjutkan dengan percikan keberanian untuk menyalakan potensi kreatif bangsa, dan berpuncak pada pertaruhan besar untuk meluruskan kembali neraca keadilan negeri, mungkin belum sepenuhnya selesai. Masih banyak pekerjaan rumah yang menanti. Tapi setidaknya malam ini, di bawah langit Jakarta yang berbintang, ia bisa merasa bahwa arah kompas bangsa ini kini telah menunjuk lebih mantap pada cita-cita luhur supremasi hukum yang sesungguhnya. Dan ia siap melanjutkan perjalanan itu, dengan hati yang lebih bijak, jiwa yang lebih kuat, dan cinta pada negeri yang tak pernah surut. Cahaya setelah serangkaian badai itu kini bukan hanya terasa hangat menenangkan, tapi juga menjadi obor penerang jalan panjang di depan mereka.

1: Istana Negara, Jakarta – A Few Months After the Family Readiness Bill's Passage (Around Mid-2045)

Jakarta's sky that afternoon burned crimson, its warm glow reflecting off the row of tall windows in the President's Office at Istana Negara. Several months had rolled by since the Speaker's gavel struck at the Parliament building, passing the Family Readiness Bill into Law after such a fierce, emotionally draining political fight. The most brutal political storm ever to hit Nisa Farha's administration had now subsided, replaced by the busyness of implementing the new policy — more measured, more technical, but no less complex.

On President Nisa Farha's always-tidy mahogany desk, the stack of documents now held more early evaluation reports from BKKBN and the Ministry of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection, drafts of implementing regulations derived from the Family Law, and schedules for intensive outreach to regions still showing resistance. Nisa had just signed the last disposition sheet for the day, stretching her stiff shoulders slightly. A cup of jasmine tea, starting to cool, stood loyally beside her, its soft aroma nearly swallowed by the distinctive smell of document paper and the constant cold air from the AC. There was a faint but real relief in the afternoon air. The relief of a captain who'd managed to steer his ship through the worst storm's fury, even knowing the ocean ahead still held many challenges.

A thin, sincere smile crossed Nisa's lips as her eyes caught a brief report from Angel Marina on her tablet screen. The report contained fairly positive initial responses from several women's groups and family counseling institutions toward the pre-marital counseling program just beginning to run as part of the law's implementation in several pilot cities. At least, that first, hardest, most controversial step had begun to bear small buds of hope.

But that satisfied smile didn't last long on Nisa's face. Her gaze shifted to another report lying on the desk, a periodic report prepared by Anton Prasetya, her Special Staff for Social Affairs and Community Empowerment. The report contained quarterly data on young workforce participation trends and developments in several priority economic sectors, including the creative economy sector Nisa always considered one of the keys to Indonesia's future. Those statistical figures, though presented in bright colorful graphs and attractive infographics, whispered a different kind of unease into Nisa's mind.

Something felt off. Growth in several key creative subsectors — like animation, mobile app development, graphic design, even digital content creation — looked stagnant, some even showing a slight decline compared to the optimistic projections made after last year's creative economy stimulus launch. Yet data from the Ministry of Education she held showed the opposite: interest in studying related majors (Visual Communication Design, Animation, Computer Science) had actually risen significantly, graduate numbers had increased, and various supporting facilities like startup incubators or shared creative spaces were popping up in many cities.

Nisa furrowed her brow. There's an odd mismatch here, she thought. Great potential seems to be hitting an invisible wall. We have so much young talent, high interest, and we're slowly improving educational infrastructure. But why does industry absorption, especially at the level requiring original innovation and the creation of genuine Indonesian intellectual property, feel so slow? Why do we still tend to be a big consumer market rather than a respected producer of creative content or technology?

“There seems to be an anomaly, doesn't there, Madam President?” Anton Prasetya's calm voice suddenly sounded from the office doorway, as if reading Nisa's mind. Her always-analytical special staff had just come in quietly to fetch another document needing follow-up, but his sharp eyes caught Nisa's expression fixed on the report he'd prepared.

Nisa raised her face, a little startled but nodding slowly. “Yes, Anton. Quite an anomaly,” she answered. She invited Anton to sit for a moment in the guest chair in front of her desk. “I've been thinking about this. We have so much potential young talent, their interest in the creative industry is very high, we're slowly improving educational facilities and early support together with related ministries. But why does industry absorption, especially work requiring original innovation and the courage to take risks, feel slow? Why does it feel like we're still more of a market for creative products from abroad, rather than a producer whose work goes global?”

Anton adjusted his thick black-framed glasses, a habit of his when about to deliver in-depth analysis. “Several initial analyses from our team in the field, ma'am,” he began, “of course beyond classic issues like still-limited access to venture capital or the challenge of penetrating global market networks, we've found strong indications that a non-economic factor plays a significant role.”

“A non-economic factor?” Nisa repeated, interested. “That's right, ma'am,” Anton continued. “A kind of... collective doubt? Or perhaps more precisely, widespread insecurity among our young creators?” He opened his tablet, showing some supporting data. “Social media sentiment analysis and discussions in creators' online forums show a fairly high level of insecurity. There are so many young talents who are actually very gifted, with brilliant ideas, but they don't dare release their own original work to the public.”

“Don't dare? Why?” Nisa asked, curious. “Various reasons, ma'am,” Anton answered. “Afraid of being judged by netizens or fellow creators. Afraid their work is considered not good enough, not up to 'international standards.' Afraid of total failure and embarrassment. Afraid of not being as 'cool' as the currently popular global trend. As a result,” Anton concluded, “many of them end up choosing the 'safe' path: becoming freelancers for foreign projects with clear specifications, or simply copying global trends wholesale that are guaranteed to sell in the market, rather than struggling to create something truly new and original from our own identity.”

Nisa was silent for quite a while, digesting Anton's words that felt so on point. Collective doubt. Insecurity. Fear of judgment. Fear of failure. Fear of not being as good as international standards. Those terms resonated strongly with something she'd vaguely felt herself lately, not just from the statistical data on paper, but also from her sporadic interactions outside the Palace circle.

She remembered her brief conversation with several talented young filmmakers at a film festival a few weeks ago. Their enthusiasm burned so brightly when discussing cinematography techniques or the visual effects of the latest Hollywood films. But that enthusiasm seemed to dim, replaced by a hesitant tone or vague diplomatic answers, when Nisa asked about their own film projects trying to tell local folk stories or social issues in their regions. There was a kind of subtle but very real lack of self-confidence, as if they felt stories from their own country were 'less sellable' or 'less prestigious' compared to stories from abroad.

“Thank you for this very interesting initial analysis, Anton,” Nisa said finally, breaking the silence. Her gaze now refocused, a new complex problem beginning to form in her mind. “Please deepen this study further. I want a more comprehensive mapping. Where exactly is the root of this mentality problem? Is something wrong with our education system that might overemphasize memorization and uniformity, undervaluing originality and the courage to try? Or is this a result of our sociocultural pressure, which might be too communal and give too little room for different individual expression? Or maybe... is this a deeper inferior mentality inheritance from the past that we haven't fully overcome?”

Anton nodded in understanding, noting Nisa's instruction points on his tablet. “Understood, Madam President. We'll follow up immediately with a more in-depth study, involving social psychology and education experts if needed too.”

After Anton left the room, Nisa looked back at the creative economy report on her desk, but her mind now drifted far beyond the growth figures and statistical graphs. A law like the Family Readiness Bill could regulate behavior, could set standards. Economic policy could provide financial stimulus. But how do you regulate — or more precisely, liberate — a nation's self-belief? How do you grow the courage to create with an authentic voice in the heart of every young person? That question felt far more complicated and fundamental.
Two Days Later – Faculty of Fine Arts and Design (FSRD) Hall, Prominent State University, Jakarta

Nisa made time in her packed schedule to attend the opening of a Student Thesis Exhibition at the Faculty of Fine Arts and Design at a prominent state university in Jakarta. Her presence was more personal, fulfilling an old invitation from the university's Rector, who happened to be a close friend of hers since college, and also as a real form of support for Indonesia's young creative generation. She deliberately requested minimal presidential protocol, accompanied only by a few aides and blended-in security, trying to be able to see the works up close, feeling firsthand the pulse of their creativity.

The faculty's large hall pulsed with overflowing youthful energy. Brightly colored canvases with various painting styles hung on white panels. Provocative, thought-provoking conceptual art installations stood in several corners. Digital screens displayed short animations, interactive designs, and dynamic graphic design portfolios. There was also a special corner for photography exhibits and innovative industrial product design prototypes.

Nisa walked slowly from one work to another, accompanied by the Rector and Dean of the faculty, who looked proud. She listened with great interest to the students' explanations of the concepts behind their work, occasionally asking questions showing sincere appreciation and understanding of the art world.

Many works were technically stunning. The students' skill in handling medium, both traditional and digital, was beyond doubt. Many ideas were also fresh and interesting. But Nisa couldn't ignore the odd feeling that gripped her heart again, the same feeling as when she read Anton's report two days ago. Amid all that technical brilliance and fresh ideas, there was a kind of thin layer of uniformity in their courage. Many technically brilliant works still felt 'safe,' very clearly referencing international visual trends or styles currently popular on platforms like Behance or Pinterest. Those that truly tried to break the mold, raising specific local issues with a very personal and unique visual style, felt fewer in number. And often, those 'different' works were placed in less strategic corners of the exhibition, as if hesitant to display them up front.

Nisa's steps suddenly stopped in front of a large monitor screen displaying a series of digital illustrations so vivid and captivating. The work depicted a scene of a traditional Indonesian night market, perhaps in a small Javanese town, but with a touch of magical surrealism that made it feel special. The detail was extraordinary — from the poetic twinkle of colorful ting lamps hung among vendor tents, the richly characterized facial expressions of sellers and visitors (some laughing, some tired, some full of hope), the bustling atmosphere that felt almost audible, to the presence of small mythological creatures — perhaps a tuyul or forest fairy? — that seemed to hide shyly among the crowd, adding a unique fantasy element. The color palette also felt different, warm, slightly somber yet magical, not following the pastel or bright neon color trends currently dominating graphic design on social media. There was such a strong visual identity there. An original voice, daring to tell its own story in its own style.
“This... is extraordinary,” Nisa murmured softly, her eyes glued to the amazing details on the screen.

A petite female student, wearing a simple flannel shirt and a calm-colored headscarf, stood nervously beside that work's installation. Her face mostly looked down, her fingers tightly interlaced in front of her body. She was the creator, named Rini, as stated on the small plaque below the monitor screen.
Nisa turned to her, giving her warmest, most sincere smile. “Rini, congratulations. Your work here... truly has 'soul,'” Nisa said, her voice full of appreciation.

Rini raised her face instantly, looking extraordinarily shocked to be addressed directly by the President of the Republic of Indonesia. Her cheeks flushed deep red from a mix of nervousness, shock, and perhaps a little pride she tried to hide. “Th-thank you very much, Madam President,” she answered haltingly, her voice barely audible from how soft it was. She looked down again. “But... this... this is nothing special, ma'am. Still has so many flaws.”

Nisa smiled gently, trying to calm the girl's nervousness. “Nothing special? I don't think so, Rini,” Nisa replied. “Your digital technique is already very mature and the detail is extraordinary. But more importantly, you have a very unique and strong visual storytelling style. You've managed to capture the essence of a typical Indonesian night market atmosphere, but with a new and fresh magical touch. This is not ordinary at all. This is special.”

Instead of looking happy or proud hearing such high praise from a president, Rini instead looked even more downcast, her fingers interlacing even tighter until her knuckles whitened. “Ah, not really, ma'am,” she answered softly, almost whispering. “This was just a thesis, I just drew this theme for fun. I also looked at a lot of references from foreign illustrators, ma'am. Their work is far better, more... cool. Their technique is more advanced, their ideas crazier. I'm still nothing compared to them.”

She paused for a moment, then added in an even softer voice, as if admitting an embarrassing secret. “I also... actually didn't dare display this illustration series at first, ma'am,” she admitted. “Afraid... afraid of looking weird. Afraid of being criticized by friends or lecturers. Afraid of being called tacky or not up to date with current design trends...”

Nisa's heart sank hearing that innocent admission laden with such deep self-doubt. This young woman before her had extraordinary talent, able to create work this strong and original, yet she herself couldn't see the value of her own work. She was trapped in a trap of endless comparison with 'foreign standards' she considered superior. She felt inferior, worthless, and paralyzed by fear of others' judgment.

This is no longer just a statistical data anomaly, Nisa thought bitterly. This is a real mentality wound. A deep wound. A wound that might have unconsciously hindered this nation's best potential from shining with its own color and voice on the world stage.

Nisa tried giving Rini a few more encouraging words, reassuring her once more of her work's value and uniqueness. But she knew, her momentary words of encouragement wouldn't be enough to heal a self-doubt wound that seemed so deeply rooted. There was something deeper, more systemic, that needed fixing in this country.

She left the art exhibition some time later with strong mixed feelings: sincere admiration for the extraordinary potential she'd just witnessed, but also deep bitterness seeing how that potential was overshadowed by a dark cloud of self-doubt. The brief but piercing conversation with Rini kept echoing in her mind throughout the journey back to the Palace.

This is no longer just a creative economy issue. This is a nation's self-confidence issue. And Nisa began to feel, this was the next battlefield she had to enter. A battlefield perhaps invisible, but no less important for Indonesia's future. She had to find a way to plant that seed of courage in a field of doubt that looked so vast.
2: Istana Negara, Jakarta – A Few Weeks After the Visit to the FSRD Exhibition (Around July–August 2045)

The seed of an idea planted in Nisa Farha's mind after her heart-piercing conversation with Rini, the young illustrator, a few weeks ago, had now begun to sprout and take shape. Her unease about the 'confidence deficit' locking up the nation's creative potential was no longer just a private nighttime reflection or an intimate discussion with Reza. That unease had crystallized into an initial concept, a draft of thinking ready for her to fight for and sharpen together with her closest circle of power.

Today, Nisa gathered several key ministers and her core staff in the Palace's Limited Meeting Room. Unlike the formal, spacious Cabinet Meeting Room, this room felt more intimate, designed specifically for strategic discussions requiring deep thinking and freer exchange of ideas. A large round table dominated the room, allowing all participants to face each other directly. Besides Anton Prasetya and Angel Marina, already involved from the start in diagnosing the problem, also present was the Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs, Pak Purnomo, his face always looking serious analyzing figures and fiscal impact. Beside him sat the Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology, Mas Farrel (a progressive figure), known for his great enthusiasm on human resource development issues and always open to policy innovation. Also present was the Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy, Ibu Wulan, an energetic figure whose portfolio was most directly affected by this issue and always eager to seek new opportunities. Not to be forgotten, the Minister of Communication and Information, Pak Hartono, who tended to be more cautious, always thinking of regulatory implications and the wild dynamics of digital space.

The atmosphere felt slightly different from the usual economic or political policy meetings they attended. There was a layer of anticipation and a bit of confusion in the air. This meeting's invitation carried an unusual agenda, even seeming abstract to some ministers: “Strengthening the National Creative Ecosystem Through a Mental Wellbeing and Courage-to-Create Approach.”

Nisa opened the meeting calmly, greeting each minister and staff member one by one with her warm smile that nonetheless carried seriousness. Her eyes radiated strong conviction about the urgency of the issue she was about to raise. She wasted no time, immediately inviting Anton Prasetya to present the more comprehensive data findings, the result of several weeks of deepening.

The large screen on the room's wall displayed graphs and data analyses confirming and sharpening Anton's initial findings. Indonesia's great creative talent potential was clear from data on the number of art and design students, participation in online creative communities, and domestic market growth for popular cultural products. But that data was juxtaposed with another contrasting fact: the dominance of imported works in cinemas and streaming platforms, the low contribution of original Indonesian IP (Intellectual Property) to the global market, and independent survey results showing high levels of anxiety, burnout, and impostor syndrome reported by young creators. Anton also presented a more detailed social media sentiment analysis: sharp polarization in responding to local work — between blind fanatical support and destructive criticism that often personally attacked the creator — creating a climate very unconducive to experimentation and creative risk-taking.

After that cold but stirring data presentation ended, Nisa took over. She didn't just talk about numbers and graphs. In a more personal tone, she shared again her experience meeting Rini at the art exhibition the other day — the digital illustrator girl with extraordinary talent who instead felt her work was 'nothing special,' 'nothing at all,' and too afraid of others' judgment.

“Honorable ministers,” Nisa began, her clear but weighty voice filling the room. “The data Anton just presented certainly worries all of us from the economic and national competitiveness side. But what worries me more personally,” she paused briefly, looking at each face before her, “are the human stories behind those numbers. Stories about the potential of our young people locked tightly by self-doubt. Stories about unique voices from our culture that might never be heard on the world stage because their creators are too afraid of judgment, too afraid of failure, or too afraid of being considered not up to some 'standard' set by who-knows-who.”

She let her words sink in. “We cannot build the Golden Indonesia we aspire to just by building toll roads and ports, just by maintaining macroeconomic stability, if the human mental and spiritual foundation is fragile,” she continued. “If our next generation doesn't have the courage to dream big, try new things, voice original ideas, and even learn from failure. Creativity and innovation are the future's currency, and both need courage as fuel.”

“Therefore,” Nisa straightened her posture, her eyes now glowing with familiar spirit, “I want to propose a step beyond just an ordinary program. I want us to start a national movement. A joint effort to reignite the spark of courage in the hearts of our creators, our innovators, from Sabang to Merauke. From those working in sophisticated studios in the capital, to those working in simple workshops in remote villages.” She smiled thinly. “I'm calling it, for now... 'Bold Spark.'”

A moment of silence followed Nisa's announcement. The ministers seemed to digest an idea that sounded quite philosophical and different from the usual cabinet meeting agenda. Coordinating Minister Purnomo, the first to speak, his tone as usual full of pragmatic consideration. “A very noble and inspiring vision, Madam President,” Pak Purnomo began carefully. “However, allow me to ask from a side that might sound less poetic. How will we measure the return on investment of a 'confidence'? Amid limited state budget and so many other urgent development priorities — infrastructure, health, basic education — how can we convince the public, and especially our colleagues in Parliament later, that investing in something as abstract as 'the courage to create' is a strategic step with measurable results?”

Before Nisa could answer that fundamental question, Minister of Education Mas Farrel interrupted with overflowing enthusiasm. “This is exactly why it's very strategic, Pak Menko, Madam President!” he exclaimed. “This aligns perfectly with the spirit of Independent Learning we're rolling out! We need to break the old mindset in our education system that often unconsciously kills creativity and only focuses on the final result in the form of numerical grades, not on the process of self-discovery and character building.” He looked at Nisa. “Building self-worth, mental resilience, and the courage to take risks early in school is the key to this nation's future. I strongly support it if there's a concrete program from this movement that can be synergized directly with the independent curriculum, extracurricular activities, or our digital education platform.”

Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy Ibu Wulan chimed in with her quick, energetic speaking style. “Completely agree, Mas Farrel! Madam President, honorable ministers, our creative economy potential is truly a sleeping giant!” “Film, music, games, fashion, culinary, crafts — we have extraordinary potential. But honestly, we often lose in the global market not merely because of technical quality, but because of this 'dare to stand out' mentality. The courage to tell our own local stories, market our original products with confidence. This is what still needs honing together.” She smiled broadly. “If this 'Bold Spark' movement can ignite that, wow... the impact on tourism, on the nation's image in the world's eyes, will be extraordinarily powerful!”

Minister of Communication and Information Pak Hartono nodded in agreement hearing his two colleagues' enthusiasm, but he quickly added a note of caution characteristic of him. “I fully agree with its positive potential, Madam President, fellow ministers,” he said. “However, we also have to be realistic about our current digital space condition, which is very noisy, often cruel, and full of traps. Encouraging the greatest courage of expression must be balanced in parallel with massive digital literacy strengthening and clear digital ethics enforcement.” He looked at Nisa. “How do we ensure this 'bold spark' doesn't instead ignite an even bigger fire of negative content? How do we prevent it from becoming a justification for spreading hoaxes, cyberbullying, or violating others' privacy in the name of 'freedom of expression'? We need a very clear and solid ethical and responsibility framework from the start.” Nisa smiled hearing that rich variety of perspectives — from budget concerns, educational enthusiasm, economic potential, to warnings about digital risks. “Thank you very much for your input and perspectives, everyone. I greatly appreciate it,” Nisa said sincerely. “And I fully agree. This isn't just about how we ignite the fire of courage, but also how we ensure that fire warms and illuminates, rather than burning down our own house.” She looked around. “That's why, after hearing Pak Hartono's input and reflecting again on its potential negative excesses, I want to propose refining this movement's name and concept. We can't just push 'Bold Spark' without clear fences. Courage must always walk hand in hand with responsibility. Therefore, I want this movement to stand on two equally strong pillars: Creative Empowerment and Ethical Responsibility. And let's refine the movement's name to: 'Bold Spark, Guard the Values,'” Nisa stated firmly.

The new name felt more complete, more balanced. The ministers nodded in agreement. Nisa then assigned them to immediately form an interministerial task force, co-led by the Minister of Education and the Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy, with full support from the Coordinating Ministry of Economic Affairs and the Ministry of Communication and Information, and involving Anton and Angel from the Palace team. Their task was clear: within the next two weeks, formulate concrete, measurable, inclusive, easily accessible program pillars, and most importantly, with a strong ethics and responsibility framework, to be presented again to the president.
The meeting closed with a new but controlled sense of optimism, though everyone was aware that implementing this big idea wouldn't be easy.
SCBD, South Jakarta – The Same Day, Afternoon

In another part of the city, in a modern glass office building in the elite SCBD area, Reza Satria was leading a board of directors meeting for the technology division of Reza Satria Group, his investment holding company whose portfolio spanned from technology to infrastructure and energy. The main agenda for that afternoon's meeting was discussing the final acquisition proposal for a local education technology (EdTech) startup considered very innovative in developing an AI-based adaptive learning platform for high school students. The due diligence team's presentation, led by Reza's head of investments, was very positive in terms of product quality, large domestic market potential, and business scalability. However, there was one small note that snagged in the founders' profile analysis section.
“What does that mean, that note about the founders' profile?” Reza asked directly, looking straight at his head of investment team, a smart young man who was a foreign university graduate.

“It means, Pak Reza,” the team head answered a bit carefully, “in terms of product, they're ready to compete. In terms of technical team, they're very solid. But we're a little worried, these founders — though technically brilliant — seem to lack an appetite or big vision for aggressive expansion into regional or global markets in the near future. Their presentation to us yesterday was very solid explaining the product and Indonesian market, but lacked 'bite' when talking long-term vision abroad. Compared to some similar EdTech startups from Singapore or Vietnam whose proposals we've seen, their level of confidence to go international feels different, sir.”

Reza was silent for a moment, absorbing that explanation. His team head's words — lacking appetite for global expansion, different confidence level — unconsciously reminded him of the discussion with Nisa last night about the 'confidence deficit' and 'inferiority mentality' hindering young creators. It turned out this phenomenon wasn't only happening in the world of art or digital content, but also in the world of technology startups that should be the most dynamic and daring. He saw its manifestation now from a very real business perspective. “Is the product good?” Reza asked again, confirming the core issue.
“Very good, sir. Very solutive for the personal learning challenges in our education system,” the team head answered firmly.
“Is the technical team solid?”
“Very solid. Technically very competent.”
“Just lacking confidence for bigger dreams and competing on the global stage?”
“More or less that's our conclusion, sir.”

Reza smiled thinly, a quick decision forming in his mind. “In that case,” he said firmly, “that's not a fundamental problem in their product or core team. That's a mindset problem. And that mindset we can shape, we can push, we can give the right 'vitamins.'” He looked at his board of directors. “We proceed with the acquisition as planned,” he decided. “But,” he added, “I want the investment team to also prepare an intensive mentorship program specifically for these founders after the acquisition completes. Involve international branding experts from our network, connect them with the global startup ecosystem we have, invite them to join major technology conferences abroad. We inject not just financial capital, but also 'vitamins of courage' and global vision.”

His decision was met with nods of agreement from the rest of the board. After the meeting ended, Reza took time in his office to call several senior business colleagues he knew had personal concern for human resource development, art, or education issues in Indonesia. He told them, in broad strokes — without leaking government plan details — Nisa's vision for a national movement to grow courage in creating and innovating among the younger generation. He explored the possibility of synergy or collaboration between this government initiative and CSR programs or foundations owned by his colleagues. The response he received turned out to be very positive. Some were interested in providing quality internship programs for young creators graduating from the government program later. Others were ready to become business or technology mentors for potential creative startups. There were also those interested in helping fund independent creative work competitions focused on originality and Indonesian values.

Reza felt the positive energy from Nisa's vision starting to spread to him and his network too. He saw real potential in an idea that might initially have sounded somewhat abstract, that it could be concretely supported by the private sector's strength. He immediately sent a short message to Nisa: “Initial exploration with a few friends about 'Spark' was very positive, love. Many interested in supporting. Let me know if you need further help.”
Istana Negara, Jakarta – Two Weeks Later

The interministerial task force met again with President Nisa Farha in the Limited Meeting Room. This time, Reza Satria was also present, not in his official capacity as the president's husband, but as a representation of the private sector support potential he'd explored. This time's presentation from the task force was far more concrete and structured than the initial discussion two weeks ago. Four main pillars of the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” program began forming clearly:

Creative & Mental Accelerator: A series of intensive bootcamps to be held in various cities (not only Jakarta). This program will combine practical skills workshops badly needed by creators (such as digital marketing, IP management, investor pitching techniques, financial literacy specific to creative workers) with group sessions and individual counseling with professional psychologists or counselors. The dual purpose: honing skills while also building mental resilience, helping creators manage criticism healthily, overcome impostor syndrome that often haunts them, and find their authentic voice in creating.

Spark Fund: A micro-grant scheme designed to be easily accessible for individual creators or small groups, especially beginners. The application process is made simple through an online platform, with assessment focused on idea originality, social or cultural impact potential, and commitment to the Guard the Values Charter, rather than a complicated business proposal. This fund is intended to finance early creative projects in various fields — from short films, independent music recordings, educational app or game development, fiction or nonfiction script writing, product design based on local wisdom, to unique regional culinary innovation. There's special emphasis on reaching creators from remote regions or marginalized groups that have historically found it difficult to access funding.

Bold Stage: Development of a physical and digital platform to give space for expression and visibility to creators, especially those involved in the Accelerator program or receiving Spark Fund. The physical platform in the form of revitalizing or building community creative hubs in several strategic regions not yet reached by similar facilities. The digital platform in the form of a curated web portal to showcase selected works, as well as utilizing the Palace's social media channels to feature inspiring creator profiles. Additionally, strategic partnerships will be forged with mainstream mass media and existing digital platforms (like YouTube, Spotify, local marketplace platforms) for broader work amplification.

Guard the Values Charter: This is the ethical pillar that becomes the movement's foundation. A joint formulation of a charter of ethics and creator responsibility in the digital age will be carried out, involving various stakeholders: Ministry of Communication and Information, Press Council, creator professional associations (film, music, design, etc.), communication and law academics, community leaders, and representatives of the creator community itself. This charter will cover clear, mutually agreed points about anti-plagiarism principles, anti-hoax and disinformation, anti-cyberbullying and doxing, respect for diversity (ethnicity, religion, race, intergroup relations), and responsible use of personal data. Signing a commitment to this charter will become one requirement to access the Spark Fund and Bold Stage facilities.

The discussion after the presentation was dynamic and constructive. Reza gave important input so that the Spark Fund funding scheme wouldn't only depend on the limited state budget, but also be designed to attract venture capital or angel investor interest focused on the creative economy, perhaps with a matching fund scheme or special showcase for Accelerator graduates. Anton highlighted again the importance of setting clear Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for each pillar, not only quantitative ones (number of works, revenue, number of followers), but also qualitative ones harder to measure, such as changes in creators' mindset, level of collaboration among creators, decrease in negative sentiment in digital space related to local work, or increase in the happiness/mental wellbeing index score of assisted creators. Angel emphasized the importance of a sustainable and consistent communication strategy, which must continuously echo the two sides of this movement's coin: a strong push to dare to create and express, along with the inseparable obligation to be responsible and guard values in every work produced. Minister of Communication and Information Pak Hartono proposed that a fast and transparent reporting and handling mechanism be designed immediately for works indicated to violate the Guard the Values Charter, involving an Independent Monitoring Team that might need to be formed later.

Nisa listened to all that input carefully, giving direction at several points, and making several key decisions. She strongly emphasized that this program should feel organic, growing bottom-up, not entirely top-down instruction. “Involve the community as much as possible in formulating program details, especially in drafting the Guard the Values Charter,” she instructed. “Don't let that charter feel like a rigid rule from the Palace, but truly a joint agreement from the ecosystem to create a healthier and more dignified creative environment for everyone.” She also emphasized again the importance of program accessibility, especially for creators outside major economic centers or from less fortunate backgrounds.
The meeting ended with a far more solid and detailed program framework. Nisa's seed idea now had roots, a stem, and a design of branches ready to grow.
A Few Days Later

Angel Marina and her communications team began running the initial-phase communication strategy, a soft launch to introduce the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” idea to the public. There was no big official launch yet, but the Palace released a short video, about one minute long, on the Presidency's official social media channels (YouTube, Instagram, X). The video showed a compilation of neatly and movingly edited footage: showing the diversity of the nation's inspiring works from various fields — clips of local animation whose quality matched foreign studios, contemporary ethnic musicians performing stunningly on the world stage, young designers turning traditional woven fabric into beautiful modern fashion, to unique culinary innovations from various regions. Those proud visual clips were interspersed with Nisa Farha's own voice narration, sounding reflective and full of empathy:

“In every corner of this country, from Sabang to Merauke, extraordinary creative potential is stored. Abundant talent, unique ideas, burning spirit. But sometimes... that potential sleeps. Sometimes... that voice falls silent. Blocked by a thin layer of doubt. Whispers of 'am I worthy?', 'is my work good enough?', 'does my voice deserve to be heard?'...”

The video then closed with a teaser about a new national movement coming soon. “...It's time to reignite that spark of courage in all our hearts. The courage to create with our own voice. The courage to become our whole selves. But courage that always walks hand in hand with responsibility. Let's together light the spark of the courage to create, while together guarding the nation's noble values.” The final screen displayed the movement's temporary logo — a dynamic, colorful spark — and a hashtag beginning to be introduced: #PercikanBerani (#BoldSpark).
That short video quickly caught public attention online. Social media algorithms carried it to the feeds of thousands, even millions of users.

In a cramped but tidy boarding room in Yogyakarta, Maya, the digital illustrator Nisa met at the FSRD exhibition, saw that video on her phone screen while taking a break from working on a freelance illustration project. Her heart pounded harder hearing Nisa's voice narration, as if speaking directly to her. Ignite the spark of courage? A familiar fear and a strange glimmer of hope appeared together in her heart. Can I do it? Do I dare?

In another corner of the noisy capital Jakarta, under the overpass where he usually rested, Bima, the street musician who'd just once again been 'secured' by the Public Order Agency because his song lyrics were considered too critical while busking near an elite office complex, saw that video on a fellow busker friend's beat-up phone. He scoffed cynically at first. “Bold Spark? Or Repression Spark?” he muttered inwardly. But somehow, the words 'stage' and 'voice' in Nisa's narration tickled his buried curiosity slightly, hidden behind his skeptical attitude.

Meanwhile, in her simple but clean kitchen in Surabaya, Ibu Santi, who was carefully arranging orders of her innovative rainbow layered cake, was shown that video by her daughter, Anisa, who'd just come home from college. Ibu Santi's tears nearly fell without her realizing it, seeing the brief footage of the struggles of culinary SME entrepreneurs in that video. She clearly remembered how the last time she tried a big online promotion for her cake, her social media account was instead swarmed relentlessly by mean comments, cruel slander, and baseless accusations until she suffered severe trauma and nearly closed her business. Guard values? she whispered inwardly. Is there anyone who can guard us from attacks that worthless and hurtful like that? A new hope appeared again in her heart, though it still felt very thin and fragile.

The initial echo from the Palace meeting room began to resonate. Reaching those who might have kept their work, their voice, and their dreams wrapped in a blanket of doubt or fear all this time. That spark began to be lit slowly. But no one yet knew how big that flame of hope would eventually blaze, and in which direction the wind of challenge and controversy would soon blow it.
3: Theater Building, Taman Ismail Marzuki (TIM), Jakarta – Official Launch Date (Around August–September 2045)

The air inside TIM's Main Theater Building pulsed with unique energy that morning — a mix of enthusiasm from young artists and creators filling the audience seats, curiosity from journalists preparing their cameras and notebooks, seriousness from government officials sitting in the front rows, and a bit of inevitable skepticism from several cultural and political observers also present. Choosing TIM as the official launch location for the National Movement “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” wasn't accidental. Nisa Farha, through direction to the Palace team, deliberately chose this place — the heart of Jakarta's art and culture ecosystem — to send a strong message that this movement was rooted in the creative world itself, not just a cold bureaucratic program born from behind a Palace desk.

The main stage was designed minimally but tastefully. Its background was just a large LED screen displaying the campaign logo: a dynamic, brightly colorful spark forming the silhouette of a growing sprout, symbolizing potential ready to bloom. Spotlights danced gently over the stage, creating a modern yet warm atmosphere. In the front row, Reza Satria sat calmly among several ministers of the United Indonesia Cabinet. His gaze was focused on the stage, a thin but supportive smile on his lips as he waited for his wife's turn to speak. He knew how Nisa had prepared this moment — not just her speech, but the whole concept of the movement born from her heart's unease. Backstage, Angel Marina gave Nisa a final boost of confidence, making sure every detail of the performance ran smoothly, while Anton Prasetya double-checked the supporting presentation materials on the program's four pillars.

After an enthusiastic opening address from Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy Ibu Wulan, who described the great potential of the creative economy if supported by a strong creator mentality, the awaited turn arrived. The host, with her melodious voice, invited the President of the Republic of Indonesia, Ibu Nisa Farha, to step up to the podium to deliver the launch speech.

Applause thundered as Nisa stepped forward from the side of the stage. She wore a modern woven blouse in bright orange radiating optimism, paired with a cream pencil skirt. Her appearance was simple yet radiated authority. She paused briefly behind the clear acrylic podium, sweeping her gaze across the whole audience — from senior artists to students, from officials to community activists. Her smile was warm as usual, but her eyes conveyed deep seriousness, a reflection of the long journey she'd taken to arrive at this idea.

“Gentlemen, ladies, brothers and sisters, activists, lovers, and doers of Indonesian creativity whom I'm proud of,” Nisa began, her voice clear and authoritative, instantly capturing the whole room's attention. “Today, we gather in a place historic to the pulse of this nation's art and culture, not merely to inaugurate a new government program. More than that, today we gather to together begin a movement. A collective effort to answer a deep unease that perhaps we've all felt, whether personally in our creative process, or as we observe this nation's pulse.”

She continued by retelling briefly, without explicitly naming Rini, her meeting with the highly talented art student who so doubted the value of her own work. She connected that personal story with data showing the great creative potential of the nation's children, often still buried or not yet reaching its peak.

“We are blessed by God Almighty with extraordinarily rich cultural diversity, abundant artistic talent and innovation in every corner of this country,” Nisa said, her tone full of appreciation. “Yet, too often I see, we hear, or we ourselves feel, a thin layer of doubt that seems to hold that golden potential back from blooming fully.
