A subtle whisper within: 'Am I worthy?', 'Is my work good enough compared to global standards?', 'Is my different voice worth hearing, or will it just be mocked?'” She paused, letting the audience reflect. “A collective 'confidence deficit,' an insecurity that may unknowingly have limited our own steps to fly higher.”

Nisa looked at the audience with a gaze now burning brighter, full of conviction. “This doubt, brothers and sisters, isn't just a matter of disturbing personal feeling,” she asserted. “It's a matter of our nation's economy losing billions in potential income from original innovation never born. It's a matter of our cultural identity that could erode further if we keep being only consumers or imitators of global trends without daring to offer our own colors. And it's also a matter of our next generation's mental health, burdened by pressure to always be perfect and paralyzed by fear of others' judgment.” “That is why,” her voice now rose full of spirit, “on the basis of that concern and great hope, today, praying for the blessing of God Almighty, saying Bismillahirahmanirrahim, we officially launch together: the National Movement 'Bold Spark, Guard the Values!'”

Applause sounded again, this time more enthusiastic and longer than before. Nisa smiled receiving that positive response, then continued explaining plainly and understandably the four main pillars that would support the movement: Creative and Mental Accelerator as a forge to hammer out practical skills and steel mentality for creators; Spark Fund as easily accessible seed capital to realize original ideas without going through convoluted bureaucratic procedures; Bold Stage as a physical and digital showcase space to present the nation's works to a wider audience; and the Guard the Values Charter as a shared ethical compass formulated by the community itself.

Then, she arrived at the most crucial part of her speech, the dual message that was the heart of this movement, the message that distinguished it from an ordinary empowerment program. “However,” Nisa said, her tone now firmer again, full of measured emphasis, “I need to underline very clearly: the courage we want to ignite through this movement is not blind courage. Not wild courage without direction. Not courage to just appear different, just be sensational, or just go viral without thinking of the impact.” She looked straight at the audience, as if wanting to ensure her message reached every individual in the room. “Bold Spark must, and will always, walk side by side, hand in hand tightly with the spirit of Guard the Values.”

“We want every Indonesian creator to dare to leap higher than before,” she continued, using a metaphor she'd once discussed with Reza. “Dare to try new things never thought of before. Dare to voice their unique perspective that might differ from the majority. But, at the same time,” she emphasized, “we also want to ensure they know how to land safely and responsibly after that daring leap. We want the nation's works to not only dazzle the world with their beauty or sophistication, but also bring goodness, enlighten shared life, and strengthen our unity as a nation.”

She paused briefly. “Freedom of expression without ethics and responsibility is destructive digital anarchy. Conversely, ethics without the courage to create and innovate is stagnation that kills our best potential.”

“The Guard the Values Charter that is and will continue to be formulated together with all elements of the creative community,” Nisa continued, “is not intended as a new government censorship tool. Not at all.” She shook her head firmly. “This charter is our shared mirror. A collective reminder that behind every work we produce, there's real impact on others. Behind every freedom we enjoy, there's accompanying responsibility. Responsibility not to spread lies or hoaxes. Responsibility not to plagiarize others' work. Responsibility not to cyberbully or personally attack discussion opponents. Responsibility not to manipulate data for momentary gain. And responsibility to always uphold the noble values of humanity, diversity, and our Indonesian-ness.”

Nisa ended her speech with a sincere and stirring invitation. “Let's make Indonesia a comfortable home, a safe home, a fertile home for brilliant ideas to grow and develop,” she said. “A place where every child of this nation, from Sabang to Merauke, feels safe and confident to light their own bold spark. And do it in a way that makes us all proud, an ethical way, a responsible way.” She smiled broadly. “Let's create boldly, let's guard our noble values together, for an Indonesia that's more creative, more competitive, and more dignified in the world's eyes.”
“Thank you. Wassalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh.”

Nisa's speech closed with a standing ovation from most of the audience. It was clear Nisa's message balancing the push for courage and the enforcement of ethics had succeeded in touching and being accepted by many, though a nuance of caution and perhaps a little doubt was still felt in some corners of the room.

The press conference session held after the launch event was lively. Angel Marina and Pak Adam Ismail, the Presidential Spokesperson, calmly but sharply answered a barrage of pointed questions from journalists. The media's main focus was on the practical aspects and potential problems of this new movement: “Where does the funding come from? Is it purely the state budget or is there private funding? How big is the budget?” asked an economics journalist. “How will the Spark Fund distribution mechanism be transparent and prevent potential collusion or favoritism toward certain groups?” pressed an investigative journalist. “Then how will the Guard the Values Charter be implemented? Who will oversee compliance? What are the sanctions for violations? Doesn't this risk becoming a new form of restriction on freedom of expression?” another journalist pushed. And of course, the hardest question: “How will the Palace measure this program's success if the target is something as abstract as 'confidence' or 'courage'?”

Angel and Adam calmly answered one by one, referring to Nisa's presentation and the task force's materials. They emphasized that funding sources would come from a combination of the state budget and strategic private partnerships. The Spark Fund selection mechanism would be made transparent based on a digital platform with independent curators. Implementation of the Guard the Values Charter would involve active community participation and its enforcement would be educational and corrective, not repressive. And success measurement would focus on qualitative indicators (mindset change, work quality, social impact) besides quantitative ones (number of beneficiaries, creative economy revenue growth). They also repeatedly asserted this wasn't a free money-handout program, but a long-term investment in building a healthy creative ecosystem and superior human resources.

That night, news about the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” launch dominated online news portals and social media timelines. The headlines were very varied, reflecting polarizing opinions starting to form: “President Nisa's Ambitious Breakthrough: Injecting Creator Confidence Through National Movement” (pro-government media). “Palace Launches 'Bold Spark,' Opposition Questions Urgency and Budget Amid People's Economic Hardship” (opposition media). “Guard the Values: Nisa's Effort to Balance Freedom of Expression and Responsibility in the Digital Disruption Era” (analytical media). Down to the more cynical and dismissive: “After Handling Marriage Readiness, Now the President Wants to Handle Creators' Hurt Feelings?” (satire/buzzer account).

In her simple but clean boarding room in a corner of Yogyakarta, Maya stared at her laptop screen displaying the newly launched official “Bold Spark” website. Its design looked clean, modern, with bright colors evoking a spirit of optimism. She carefully reread the details about the Creative and Mental Accelerator pillar. Her eyes fixed on the description of a special session on “Overcoming Psychological Barriers in Creating (Imposter Syndrome, Creative Block, Fear of Judgment)” and “Building Mental Resilience Against Criticism and Hate Speech Online.” Her heart pounded a little faster. It felt like… this program was designed specifically to answer all the anxieties and fears that had paralyzed her all this time.

With slightly trembling hands, she opened the link to the online registration form for the Accelerator's first cohort. The questions seemed straightforward: personal data, a portfolio link (noted as optional for total beginners), and a short essay about her motivation to join the program and the biggest challenge faced in her creative process. Maya froze for a long time on that essay field. What should I write? she thought anxiously. Should I be completely honest about this anxiety that often paralyzes me? About my irrational fear of others' judgment? About the deep insecurity I feel seeing others' work? What if the selection committee laughs at it? Considers it too weak or 'oversensitive'? Or worse, what if she's accepted and then fails completely mid-program, embarrassing herself?

Her hands felt cold, her breath a little tight from that familiar wave of anxiety. With an abrupt, rough motion, she closed her laptop screen. No. I can't. This is too scary. I'm not ready. I'm not good enough yet. That negative thought screamed loudly in her head. However, a glimmer of hope from President Nisa's speech that afternoon, about the importance of daring to take even the smallest first step, still lingered faintly in her mind. After a few minutes of calming herself, she opened her laptop again. Not to fill out the form, but just to bookmark that registration page in her browser. Maybe… maybe tomorrow I'll try looking again, she whispered inwardly, though she herself wasn't sure whether that courage would come tomorrow.

Under the dim streetlight beneath a Jakarta overpass, Bima wiped the sweat from his forehead after a full day of busking, the earnings not much. Several fellow street musician friends gathered nearby, sharing the remains of mineral water in a grubby plastic bottle and talking about the Palace's new program launch they'd briefly seen on a TV screen at a nearby food stall.

“Hah, probably just another program like that. Just for the big shots and their cronies,” one dreadlocked friend remarked, his tone cynical. “Yeah, right. How could street people like us possibly get that Spark Fund? Just filling out the form's probably a huge hassle, not to mention the portfolio requirements and all,” another chimed in while plucking his beat-up guitar out of tune.

Bima stayed mostly silent, just listening while leaning his back against the cold concrete bridge pillar. He remembered the campaign logo he'd briefly seen on the food stall's TV screen — a colorful spark. Somehow, that logo slightly reminded him of the spirit of his own songs, often considered 'fiery' and provocative. With his beat-up phone whose screen was cracked in a thousand places, he tried searching for more information about the “Bold Stage” program. He found a list of several local art communities in Jakarta said to be the program's initial partners. One was an alternative art studio on the city's outskirts that Bima knew had a fairly good reputation, open to independent musicians from various backgrounds, and often held small but quality music events. Then his eyes landed on the explanation section about the “Guard the Values Charter.” He read it briefly: anti-hoax, anti-bullying, respect for ethnic/religious/racial differences, no personal attacks. Bima scoffed again. So ironic. He himself had often been a victim of small-scale hoaxes or verbal bullying from officials or even fellow citizens while busking, just because of his appearance or his song lyrics. But if they were really serious about this 'Guard the Values' thing, well, good, he thought inwardly. He copied and saved the contact number of that partner art studio in his not-so-large contact list. No strong intention yet to contact them soon, but at least the information was saved. A little curiosity and hope, however small, managed to beat his usually dominant cynicism that night.

Meanwhile, in a simple but pleasant house in Surabaya, Ibu Santi was discussing with her only daughter, Anisa, a communications student still fired up describing the details of the newly launched “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” program. “Look at this, Ma,” Anisa said, showing her tablet screen displaying the Creative & Mental Accelerator explanation section. “There's a special class on digital marketing strategy for culinary SMEs! And this… material on 'Building Positive Online Reputation and Crisis Management When Hit by Cyber Attacks.' This is exactly what you need after what happened last time!”

Ibu Santi looked at that tablet screen with mixed feelings. Memories of the brutal attack and cruel slander on her rainbow layered cake business's social media account a few months ago still left deep traumatic wounds. Demeaning comments about her product, accusations of using dangerous ingredients, to veiled threats that made her afraid to leave the house for weeks. She'd almost completely closed the small business she'd built with such difficulty if not for Anisa's support and some loyal customers.

“Is it really true, Nduk, that a government program could be that great?” Ibu Santi asked her daughter doubtfully. “Later the administration will get complicated, all sorts of requirements, wasting Ma's time just dealing with that stuff.”

“Just try it first, Ma! This is a great opportunity!” Anisa persuaded, not giving up. “Don't you really want Grandma's heirloom rainbow layered cake business to be known more widely? If your mental strength is stronger after the training, the digital strategy better, surely unclear attacks like last time can be faced! You mustn't keep being afraid!”

Anisa then opened the Spark Fund registration form on her tablet. “There, Ma! We can apply for this grant to make new, better and more modern packaging, or maybe to make a professional promotional video to upload on Instagram and TikTok! In the motivation essay section, we just tell your struggle all this time, how you want to build a positive and mutually supportive traditional culinary lovers' community, in line with the 'Guard the Values' spirit Madam President mentioned earlier!” Seeing her daughter's overflowing enthusiasm, and imagining her delicious cake could be known by more people without going through the same painful trauma, Ibu Santi's heart slowly began to soften. She sighed long. “Alright then, Nduk. Help me fill out the form slowly,” she finally said, giving in to Anisa's persuasion. “But don't get your hopes up too much, okay. If it doesn't get through, it's fine, no problem.”

That night, with Anisa patiently guiding and typing, Ibu Santi began pouring her family's struggle, hope, and secret recipe story onto the Spark Fund's digital form sheet. A small, doubt-filled first step, but a sign of her budding courage to step out of the fear zone that had shackled her all this time.

Elsewhere, in a very cold air-conditioned closed meeting room in a luxury office building, Pak Hardiman smiled cynically watching news clips of Nisa Farha's new campaign launch on the large TV screen on the wall. “Hmph! Bold Spark, Guard the Values?” he muttered to several opposition politician colleagues and political consultants sitting in the room. “More like Budget Spark, Guard the Image!” he sneered, met with small laughter from the others. He looked at the TV screen with a cunning gaze. “This is a golden opportunity for us. An ambitious but abstract program like this surely has many holes. Watch every rupiah of its budget later in Commission VIII. Find any small gap to attack. Let's see how long Nisa Farha's 'spark' can last before being blown out by the wind of political reality and scandal.” Several other council members in the room nodded in agreement, ready to seek new ammunition to shake the Palace's throne.

At the same time, in dark corners of cyberspace, several influential anonymous accounts affiliated with the opposition network began moving. Memes twisting the “Bold Spark” campaign logo into mocking caricatures started spreading. Long threads on platform X questioning the government's competence in handling creators' 'feelings' or 'mental health' began rolling out. Some also started subtly linking this movement to a 'cultural liberalization' agenda or a veiled 'attack on religious values.' Seeds of more organized resistance began being sown systematically, waiting for the right time to grow and cause damage.

That night, Nisa and Reza stood briefly on their private bedroom balcony before resting, watching the city lights twinkling in the distance. “The first day's response is always the loudest, huh,” Nisa said with a long sigh, lightly massaging her temples. She'd just finished reading the media summary and initial sentiment analysis from Angel on her tablet. “Grassroots enthusiasm feels quite big, lots of hope from young creators. But skepticism from observers, attacks from the opposition, and potential black campaigns are also already showing their pattern very clearly.”

Reza gently wrapped his arm around his wife's shoulder. “That was to be expected, love,” he said soothingly. “No big change comes without ripples. What matters, the message has been thrown to the public. People are starting to talk about this issue, about the importance of confidence but also responsibility. That's already a very good first step.” He smiled. “And the good news, from some of my business contacts earlier, private sector interest in getting involved in mentorship or funding programs turns out to be quite serious. They see the long-term value for talent development in their industries.”

Nisa nodded, a little relieved hearing the news from Reza. “Hopefully the collaboration can run smoothly,” she said. “But I know, the real test of this movement isn't at this festive launch event, nor at the budget figures or number of participants later. The real test is in the field.” She leaned on Reza, her gaze distant again. “Seeing whether Maya in Jogja will eventually dare to submit her form. Seeing whether Bima under that bridge finds his worthy stage. Seeing whether Ibu Santi in Surabaya can truly rise again from her trauma and grow her business. That's what will determine whether this spark truly ignites or is just a momentary firework.”

She looked at Reza. “This will be a very different journey from the bill last time, Mas,” she continued. “Last time we fought a more visible legal structure and political lobby. This time, we're trying to fight the doubt in many people's hearts, including perhaps in our own hearts. And at the same time, we also have to fight those with a stake in keeping that doubt and fear alive.”
Reza tightened his embrace. “And as always,” he whispered gently in Nisa's ear, “we'll face it all together. One spark, one value, at a time.”

They looked back at the twinkling city lights spreading below the Palace. The official launch was over. Its initial echo had sounded, reaching hope and doubt in various corners of the country. Now was the time to see how the first voices from these creators would truly resonate, and how the storm of resistance from those disturbed would begin to form and strike. A new chapter of Nisa Farha's struggle — the struggle to ignite the flame of creativity and courage in the nation's soul — was just about to begin.
4: Location (Palace, Yogyakarta, Jakarta, Surabaya) and Cyberspace – Several Months After the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” Launch (Late 2045 – Early 2046)

The first months after the National Movement's official launch at Taman Ismail Marzuki were colored by a new wave of energy welling up in Indonesia's creative ecosystem. Like dry earth finally watered by rain after a long drought, the program was welcomed with enthusiasm exceeding the Palace team's initial expectations. The campaign's official website was flooded with visitors, the Spark Fund application form was downloaded tens of thousands of times from across the country, and online and offline workshop schedules from the Creative & Mental Accelerator pillar in various pilot cities were quickly packed with registrants. New hope felt like it was blooming.

In the corner of her simple boarding room, now feeling more spacious with hope, in Yogyakarta, Maya, the digital illustrator, finally managed to conquer the wave of doubt that had paralyzed her for weeks. Pushed by the patience of her online mentor from the Accelerator program — a senior illustrator who patiently helped her break her anxiety into smaller, more manageable steps — and also by her own courage growing little by little each day, Maya finally pressed 'send' on her Spark Fund proposal. Her proposal was ambitious but full of potential: a bold narrative digital illustration series concept, reinterpreting strong women's legends from the archipelago (like Roro Jonggrang or Calon Arang) with a unique contemporary visual style, slipping in subtle social commentary on current issues like patriarchy and gender injustice.

Every time she opened her email app after that, her heart always pounded harder. Until one cloudy afternoon, the email she both awaited and feared most arrived. Its subject was short: “Spark Fund Batch 1 Initial Selection Announcement.” With trembling hands, she opened it. The first sentence leaped straight to her eyes: “Congratulations! Your proposal 'Nusantara Reimagined' has passed the Spark Fund's initial selection…”

Maya read that sentence over and over, disbelieving. Tears of joy mixed with strange panic streamed down her cheeks. She was accepted! Her dream of being able to focus on her own personal project, funded too, was coming true! But instantly, that cunning voice of doubt whispered again in her ear: Can I finish it by the deadline? What if the result turns out bad and disappoints everyone? What if people hate my interpretation of this sacred legend?

However, this time, there was another, stronger voice, a voice she'd gained from Accelerator counseling sessions and the echo of President Nisa's speech the other day: Focus on the one small step in front of you. Enjoy the process. Courage doesn't mean having no fear, but still stepping forward despite fear. Maya took a deep breath, wiped her tears, then with new resolve opened her design software and began making the first rough sketch for her version of the Roro Jonggrang comic panel. That spark began to ignite.

In bustling Jakarta, Bima, the street musician, also began feeling a small but significant change in his life. After a few times boldly performing his critical songs at small community music events held by the art studio partnering with the “Bold Stage” program, he began gaining recognition. Not from officials or major record labels, of course, but from fellow independent musicians, social activists, and a small circle of loyal community event audiences who appreciated the honesty of his lyrics and his stage energy. His sharp criticism now began to be heard in the context of art worthy of appreciation, not just a frustrated shout on the roadside worthy of being ignored or shut down.

The Spark Fund he received, though not a fantastic amount, felt like an unexpected blessing. Enough to rent a simple recording studio on Jakarta's outskirts for several full days and pay a few musician friends from the studio to help him arrange his three signature songs more maturely. The recording process itself felt magical to him. Hearing lyrics he usually just shouted with only his beat-up acoustic guitar accompaniment, now wrapped in richer music arrangement with added bass, cajon percussion, and a touch of keyboard — recorded with clear sound quality, giving him a sense of validation and pride in his work he'd never felt before. One song, titled “Rats in Neckties at the Paper Palace” — the song with the sharpest lyrics and most vulgar metaphors he wrote to criticize a bureaucracy he considered slow, corrupt, and deaf to the voice of ordinary people — sounded very powerful and biting in this demo recording version. He couldn't wait to upload it.

Meanwhile, hundreds of kilometers away in Surabaya, Ibu Santi felt a genuine fresh wind of hope blowing through her rainbow layered cake business. The Creative & Mental Accelerator workshop on digital marketing strategy, personal branding, and especially online reputation management gave her the knowledge and new confidence she badly needed. With enthusiastic help from her daughter Anisa, who helped translate that digital theory into real practice, plus the Spark Fund grant she used entirely to redesign her cake packaging into something more modern and appealing and run a more planned and interactive social media content strategy (including recipes, tips, and behind-the-scenes stories), orders for her rainbow layered cake increased drastically within a few months.

She was now far more active and confident interacting with customers online, building a small but solid community of traditional cake lovers on her business's Instagram and Facebook accounts. Encouraged by her Accelerator mentor, she even began daring to gradually share her story of fighting the cyberbullying and cruel slander she'd once endured, as part of her own version of the “Guard the Values” narrative: about the importance of building a culinary business that's not just delicious but also spreads positive energy, honesty, and a spirit of mutual support among fellow SME owners. She admitted still feeling a bit anxious every time she opened the comments section or message notifications — the shadow of that trauma wasn't easy to erase. But now, she felt far more prepared and stronger to face it, no longer alone.

Similar stories, on varying scales, emerged from other regions touched by the “Bold Spark” program. A short documentary film about fishermen's lives on the Makassar coast, made by a group of students funded by the Spark Fund, passed selection for a national-level independent film festival. A young writers' community in inland Papua, after joining a series of online writing workshops from the Accelerator, successfully self-published their first short story anthology and received a warm welcome from local readers. A Sumba ikat weaving craftsperson, helped by Bold Stage program volunteers to create a digital marketing account and online catalog, began getting direct orders from several small boutiques abroad.

Angel Marina and Anton Prasetya reported these positive developments to President Nisa Farha enthusiastically in the weekly evaluation meeting. On the Situation Room's monitor screen, program participation figures and initial positive sentiment analysis on social media looked very promising. “That spark of courage seems to be starting to catch in many places, Madam,” Angel said, her smile wide and full of optimism. Nisa smiled too, feeling genuine warmth of hope in her heart. Seeing any real impact, however small, of a policy she'd fought for was always her best fuel.

However, as a leader well-versed in facing unpredictable political and social dynamics, Nisa knew well. A newly lit fire is often the most vulnerable to a strong gust of wind or a splash of cold water called reality. And that first storm wind didn't take long to come striking, testing the foundation of this movement that was still barely a month old.

The trigger came from Bima's work, which he'd just uploaded with full pride. The demo song “Rats in Neckties at the Paper Palace,” which he uploaded via the YouTube channel of the art studio partnering with the “Bold Stage” program, turned out to have unexpected explosive power. That platform's algorithm, perhaps because of its provocative title or its raw energy, quickly carried it to a far wider audience beyond the circle of independent music communities or social activists. Initially just thousands of viewers, then tens of thousands, until within just a few days it broke through hundreds of thousands of views.

The comments section overflowed. Most praised Bima's lyrical courage, his music's honest energy, and his message considered to represent the unease and anger of many young people toward a system they considered corrupt and unjust. However, that instant popularity brought with it a sharp double-edged sword. Bima's very explicit lyrics, using rough and vulgar street language (“rats in neckties,” “bureaucracy bastards,” “thieves of the people”), metaphors considered insulting to state institutions (“paper palace”), and corruption accusations that, while perhaps voicing broad public sentiment, weren't backed by concrete investigative evidence, began drawing harsh reactions from various parties.

Several regional government officials who felt targeted openly condemned the song as “hate speech,” “cheap provocation,” and “uneducational content for the younger generation.” A youth organization known to have strong affiliation with the main opposition party even officially reported Bima and the managers of the partnering art studio to the police for alleged defamation and insult to state symbols under articles of the Criminal Code and the Electronic Information and Transactions Law.

On social media, the attacks came more brutally. Conservative groups, anonymous buzzer accounts suspected of being controlled by Nisa's political opponents, and part of the public offended by Bima's rough language began attacking en masse. They edited clips of Bima's busking performance or demo recording, framing him as a crude, uneducated street musician now funded by state money (through the Spark Fund) to insult the government and spread hatred. Negative hashtags like #StopFundingInsulters and #ChaoticSpark began appearing and being rolled out in a coordinated way to directly compete with the official hashtag #BoldSpark.

The Guard the Values Charter, the ethical pillar this movement had just tried to build, was immediately faced with its toughest test in this first case. Difficult questions arose: Did Bima's vulgar and accusation-filled lyrics violate the Charter's point on “respect for diversity and ethnic/religious/racial relations” or “anti-hoax/slander”? Must social criticism always be delivered in polite and measured language? Where exactly is the line between the freedom of expression guaranteed by the constitution and the ethical responsibility not to spread hatred or unfounded information?

Bima himself, instead of reflecting or trying to have a dialogue, reacted very harshly to the storm of criticism hitting him. To him, this harsh reaction was real proof that the system he criticized was indeed rotten, anti-criticism, and hypocritical. When a mentor from the art studio tried to approach him carefully, advising him to perhaps be more careful choosing words in his next work without losing the essence of his criticism, Bima flatly refused.

“This is my voice, man! This is the rotten reality I see and feel every day on the streets!” he shouted in a heated discussion at the art studio's headquarters. “They said this program's called 'Bold Spark,' so why am I now told to be a 'good boy'? Told to be polite facing a corrupt system? If that's how it works, this program's a lie! Just lipstick!” Not stopping there, Bima even uploaded a more provocative status on his personal social media account, which had just started gaining followers. He challenged his critics back, calling them “regime lackeys,” “morality-masked hypocrites,” or “power boot-lickers.” This explosive defensive attitude, instead of calming the situation, further muddied the waters and gave new ammunition to opponents of the “Bold Spark” program.

News about Bima's song controversy, heating up quickly, reached the ears of Nisa Farha and her team at the Palace. This was the first serious communication crisis for the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” campaign. A crisis that directly tested the dual principle forming this movement's foundation: how to balance the push to dare speak up with the obligation to still guard values? Nisa immediately instructed Angel and Anton to prepare an emergency meeting with herself, Reza, and representatives from the interministerial task force. That first storm wind came faster and stronger than she'd expected. Nisa took a long breath, looking out her office window facing the Palace's calm garden. Outside it looked peaceful, but she knew, in public space and cyberspace, a storm was raging, threatening to extinguish the spark she'd just tried to light. Her hardest task now was finding a way to keep that fire burning amid the storm, without burning down the house of hope she'd just built.
5: Various Locations (Palace, Yogyakarta, Jakarta, Surabaya) and Digital Public Space – Some Time After the Bima Controversy Subsided (Around Early 2046)

Bima's song controversy “Rats in Neckties at the Paper Palace” slowly began receding from the peak of headlines and heated public debate. Even so, the case left a lasting mark not easily erased. In online discussion spaces for independent creators, debate about the limits of social criticism, appropriate language use, and interpretation of the Guard the Values Charter continued to loom, creating a new atmosphere of caution. Bima himself, after going through tough but intensive mentoring sessions at the Bold Stage partner art studio, began trying to write new lyrics. He still kept his criticism's sharpness, but with word choices that sounded more measured, deeper metaphors, though his heart was still filled with turmoil between his raw rebellious idealism and the subtle pressure to 'play it safer.'

At Istana Negara, Anton Prasetya delivered an initial impact evaluation report on the Bima controversy to President Nisa Farha. The data showed a worrying trend: a significant drop in the number of Spark Fund proposal submissions for genres of work considered 'risky' or potentially polemic-generating, such as political satire, investigative documentary, or critical conceptual art. Conversely, proposals for works that felt 'safer' and 'more entertaining' — like cooking or makeup tutorials, generic motivational content, light slapstick comedy, or beautiful travel videos — actually increased sharply.

“The cracks are starting to show clearly, Madam President,” Anton said quietly, pointing to the proposal genre comparison graph on his tablet screen. “The Bima case controversy, even though we tried to handle it in a balanced and non-repressive way, still seems to be sending a strong 'warning' signal to other creators. The deterrent effect or chilling effect is starting to be felt clearly in the field. They're becoming more afraid to take risks.”

Nisa let out a long sigh, staring at the graph with a furrowed brow. This was exactly what she'd worried about since first formulating a response to the Bima case. Enforcing the 'Guard the Values' pillar too rigidly, or letting controversy explode uncontrolled, turned out to risk extinguishing the 'Bold Spark' flame itself, at least for a while and for some creators.

In Yogyakarta, Maya felt that deterrent effect directly in her boarding room. Her digital comic reinterpreting the Roro Jonggrang legend from a feminist perspective — depicting the Prambanan Temple princess not just as a victim of a love curse, but as an intelligent and brave figure trapped in political intrigue and her kingdom's patriarchal structure — was nearly finished for a few crucial initial panels. Its visuals were detailed, its narrative strong. Her mentor from the Accelerator program kept pushing her via short messages to submit it soon to the Digital Bold Stage platform, which was holding a monthly work selection for an online showcase.

But every time Maya opened that comic file, her stomach twisted with anxiety. The image of Bima being attacked mercilessly on social media because his song lyrics were considered 'crude' and 'insulting' kept echoing in her head. What if my work is considered 'disrespectful' of this sacred folk tale? she thought anxiously. What if some conservative cultural or religious group is offended by my interpretation? What if I'm attacked personally, my personal data spread, like I saw happen to other creators? She postponed submitting the work again. The doubt she'd managed to fight hard after receiving the Spark Fund now felt thick again like cold morning fog, paralyzing her fingers over the digital pen.

However, the real storm that would test the foundation of the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” program to its roots was just peeking over the horizon. This time, that storm came from a completely different direction, striking the 'Guard the Values' pillar from its most fundamental side: originality, information honesty, and intellectual integrity.

The eye of that storm was named Andi Saputra. An educational video content creator in his early twenties, a student at a private university in Jakarta, whose on-screen persona always looked cheerful, enthusiastic, and whose explanations of complex topics sounded so smart and easy to digest. Andi was one of the brightest 'stars' from the Creative and Mental Accelerator's first cohort, particularly in the “Building Personal Branding and Engagement on Social Media” class. Before joining the program, Andi was just an ordinary student with a social media account with few followers. But after joining the workshop a few months ago, it was as if he'd found his magic formula.

He began diligently making short explainer videos about popular science topics, unique historical facts, or current viral issues, presented in a simple animation style using ready-made templates, cheerful and catchy background music, and his characteristic fast, energetic, and convincing speaking style. His videos exploded on platforms like TikTok and YouTube Shorts. His follower count skyrocketed drastically from just thousands to hundreds of thousands within a few months. He became a new idol for many young netizens thirsty for instant information. In every interview opportunity or in his social media bio, Andi never forgot to quote the “Bold Spark” slogan and openly thank the Palace program that had given him 'confidence' and 'seed capital' (although he never actually received the Spark Fund) to dare to create and spread 'positive knowledge.' Angel Marina's communications team at the Palace even made him one of the program's early success examples in several internal promotional materials and reports to President Nisa.

One of Andi's most viral videos, the one that boosted his name the most, was his summary explanation of a popular historical conspiracy theory that had long circulated in Indonesia. In that video, under three minutes long, Andi, in his convincing style, 'debunked' that conspiracy theory using 'scientific' data and 'logical' arguments he presented with attractive animation. The video was praised profusely by many for being considered 'enlightening,' 'fighting historical hoaxes,' and presenting complex information in an enjoyable way. The video was watched millions of times across platforms, reshared by several major influencers and popular news accounts, even briefly quoted as a reference in a news program on one national TV station. Andi Saputra suddenly became a new idol, a representation of the smart, critical, and inspiring young Indonesian creator.

However, amid that praise and wave of admiration, an independent investigative journalism portal known to be very thorough, credible, and persistent in exposing public lies, published a long, in-depth report about Andi Saputra and his works. That report was the result of careful digital tracing over several weeks, involving tracing original sources, comparative analysis of text and video, and interviews with several experts in relevant fields.

The facts uncovered by that investigative report were truly shocking and stunning. Andi's viral video 'debunking' that historical conspiracy theory turned out not only to oversimplify complex historical facts to the point of being inaccurate and misleading, but most of its narrative — including several key 'scientific data' and 'logical' arguments he quoted so confidently — was the result of raw plagiarism. Andi turned out to have merely freely translated, slightly modified sentences to avoid exact matches, and repackaged content from articles in English-language academic journals with limited access for the lay public, as well as from several foreign history education creators' videos less popular in Indonesia, making their trail hard to trace. His simple animation and characteristic speaking style were just 'new packaging' for stolen content.

Even worse, that report also revealed that several other Andi videos on popular science topics were also found to contain factual misinformation or excessive oversimplification that was very misleading. Andi, in pursuit of virality, engagement, and maintaining the image of a 'smart creator' he'd built, turned out to have taken a fatal and unethical shortcut: stealing others' work and ignoring the accuracy of the information he delivered to his millions of followers.

The scandal exploded instantly in cyberspace. The hashtags #AndiPlagiat (#AndiPlagiarism) and #PercikanHoax (a twist on #PercikanBerani/#BoldSpark) immediately dominated trending topics, with an echo far bigger and more damaging than the previous Bima lyrics controversy. If the Bima case triggered debate about the limits of freedom of expression and language politeness, the Andi case struck directly at the heart of the creative and intellectual world's integrity: honesty, originality, respect for others' work, and responsibility in spreading information.

The public who had previously praised Andi now felt betrayed and deeply angry. The academic community and professional journalists launched sharp criticism against the practice of plagiarism and spreading misinformation disguised as educational content. And worst of all for Nisa and her team, the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” program's name was now dragged thoroughly through this scandal's mud. This time, the accusation was no longer just funding a creator who was insulting or impolite, but far more fundamental: accused of having promoted and produced an intellectual fraud, a misinformation spreader exploiting public trust. The 'Guard the Values' pillar just being erected felt like it collapsed instantly.

At Istana Negara, the atmosphere of the crisis meeting Nisa held that morning felt far gloomier and heavier compared to when discussing the Bima case. Nisa looked at the monitor screen showing headline news about the Andi Saputra scandal with a hardened jaw, her eyes conveying deep disappointment and restrained anger. That disappointment felt so personal to her. This was a very hard slap in her face, a blatant betrayal of the spirit of honesty and integrity she wanted to instill through the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” movement.

“This… this is absolutely intolerable,” Nisa's voice sounded cold, almost emotionless, but full of undeniable firmness. She looked at her core team. “Plagiarism is theft of intellectual property. Deliberate spread of disinformation in the name of education is public fraud. Both are fundamental violations of the Guard the Values Charter we agreed on together as this movement's foundation.” She paused briefly. “Actions like this don't just damage the reputation of the creator involved, but also damage public trust in our whole creative ecosystem, including in this program we're building with such difficulty.”

This time, there was no long debate or significant difference of opinion at the meeting table. Everyone present — Anton, Angel, ministry representatives, even Reza who was present again — agreed that firm, uncompromising action was needed to save the program's credibility and uphold principle. Reza, whose face had reddened holding back anger since reading that investigative report last night, even revealed he'd actually heard rumor whispers about the 'cheating' and 'source-grabbing' methods Andi used, from several colleagues in the digital industry some time ago, but at the time he had no concrete evidence to follow up on. “A person like this,” Reza hissed furiously, “has tarnished the reputation of thousands of other creators who work honestly and with such difficulty. He abused the 'courage' and trust given by this program just to deceive the public for instant popularity!”

The Palace quickly moved fast to issue an official statement whose tone was far harsher and firmer than when handling the Bima case. The statement strongly condemned all forms of plagiarism and spreading disinformation in creative work as unethical and unjustifiable actions. The Palace officially withdrew all forms of support and affiliation of the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” program from Andi Saputra, including removing all promotional content that had ever linked him to the program. The Palace also stated it fully supported law enforcement efforts (if there were reports from the original work's owner) or enforcement of journalistic/academic codes of ethics for this case. Furthermore, the Palace urged digital platforms (YouTube, TikTok, etc.) to take firm action according to their internal policies against Andi's account and content proven to violate rules. And as an internal corrective step, the Palace announced it would strengthen digital literacy modules, academic ethics, proper citation techniques, and respect for copyright in the Creative and Mental Accelerator workshop curriculum for subsequent cohorts. The message meant to be conveyed was very clear: The courage to create must always be accompanied by uncompromising integrity.

The impact of this firm Palace statement echoed widely. Most of the public and professional creative community welcomed the government's firm stance in maintaining ethical standards. They felt relieved that the “Bold Spark” program didn't protect a creator clearly violating fundamental principles. However, in other corners, especially in online forums for beginner creators or students, new worries and fears also emerged. Discussion now shifted to fear of unintentional 'misquoting,' worry about 'idea similarity' that might be considered plagiarism, or anxiety facing an 'originality standard' felt to be too high and hard to achieve. The fear of being judged or criticized by the public now had a new, more terrifying dimension: fear of being accused of plagiarism, a stigma that could kill a creative career even before it started.

Maya in Yogyakarta sank further into her anxiety after reading news of the Andi scandal and the Palace's firm statement. She began re-dissecting every panel of her Roro Jonggrang comic with new paranoia, searching for possible unintentional similarities in visual style or storyline with other works she'd ever seen or read. She compared her batik designs with ancient motifs, worried about being considered to be copying cultural heritage. Her creative process stalled completely, infected by a new fear virus more paralyzing than simply fearing being criticized as 'weird' or 'tacky.'

Bima, on one hand, felt a little 'safe' because at least he knew his work, however crude its lyrics, was 100% original from his own mind. However, he also witnessed how fast and hard 'punishment' from the public and institutions could be dropped on a creator considered to have crossed a line, even on someone as popular as Andi. Andi's experience made him reconsider the risk of taking on themes too controversial or sensitive in his next works, though he still insisted on the honesty of his expression.

Ibu Santi in Surabaya, conversely, actually made the Andi case a positive discussion topic in her loyal customers' online community. She re-emphasized the importance of honesty, quality raw materials, and an authentic production process in business, in line with the “Guard the Values” principles she always held firmly. To her, the Andi case actually further strengthened the relevance and urgency of the 'Guard the Values' pillar in the “Bold Spark” movement, as a reminder for all creators not to be tempted by shortcuts for false popularity.

The crack in the mirror of courage was now clearer and branching further. The program Nisa designed with the noble intent of freeing the nation's creative potential now unintentionally also sowed the seeds of a new fear just as paralyzing. Nisa Farha began to bitterly realize that building a healthy, brave, and responsible creative ecosystem simultaneously was a job far more complicated, more complex, and more full of dilemmas than simply providing a fishing hook in the form of a grant or a stage to perform on. Her homework turned out to be far bigger than she'd imagined.
6: Jakarta and Various Other Locations – Some Time After the Andi Scandal Was Uncovered (Around Mid-2046)

Two scandals exploding in close succession — the Bima lyrics controversy considered insulting, and the embarrassing Andi Saputra plagiarism case — became golden ammunition seemingly sent straight from the sky for President Nisa Farha's political opponents. Echoes of political opportunism began sounding loudly, bouncing from Parliament building meeting rooms to the most popular TV studios.

Pak Hardiman, a senior politician from the main opposition faction who never missed a chance to attack Nisa, appeared full of confidence on a prime-time political talk show, a cynical, victorious smile clear on his face. “We said it from the start! Since this idea was first floated by Madam President!” he said loudly, his hand gestures fiery in front of the camera. “This 'Bold Spark' program is a lighthouse project with unclear direction and purpose! Wasting billions of the people's rupiah just to fund impolite street provocateurs like that B fellow,” he referred to Bima, “and now it's also proven to have promoted and celebrated a plagiarist and hoax-spreader like that A fellow!” he pointed at the Andi case. He looked sharply at the camera, as if speaking directly to Nisa. “This is proof of President Nisa Farha's total failure in managing the state budget and in understanding the nation's real priority needs!”

Hardiman didn't stop there. He knew exactly how to exploit momentum. “We at Commission VIII of the House of Representatives,” he continued, referring to the commission relevant to discussing this program's budget in parliament, “will not stay silent! We'll demand a thorough evaluation and push for a significant budget cut, if necessary a total halt, for this failed program that only produces controversy and immoral creators, at the next hearing! That precious people's money is far better used to subsidize farmers' fertilizer, who are currently struggling, or for direct cash assistance for those having trouble eating, not to fund artists' social experiments that damage the nation's moral order!”

Similar narratives — failed program, budget waste, moral threat, President's incompetence — were quickly echoed by other opposition politicians across various media platforms. They systematically framed “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” as a naive, mismanaged, and even socially destabilizing program. Some even began proposing the formation of a new independent oversight board — which of course they hoped could be filled with their own people — to strictly select and monitor all content funded or facilitated by the program. A proposal subtly but clearly leading to a new-style censorship mechanism.

Pressure didn't only come from outside the Palace. Within the Palace's own circle and among Nisa's supporting coalition parties, whispers of doubt began sounding clearer. Several ministers who'd been skeptical of this program considered too 'idealistic' from the start now felt their worries proven right. Technical officials at relevant ministries, like the Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy or the Ministry of Education, became extra cautious in running the program. They tended to slow down the Spark Fund disbursement process or approval of Creative Accelerator activities in the regions, afraid of getting dragged in if new problems or controversies emerged that could endanger their careers.

Coalition party leaders, who'd already begun calculating this controversy's electoral impact ahead of the simultaneous regional head elections to be held some time ahead, informally began 'advising' Nisa. In increasingly frequent closed meetings, they suggested Nisa 'lay low' briefly regarding this program, perhaps 'revise' the program's name to something sounding 'safer' and drastically reduce its public exposure.

“The political situation is currently less favorable for a program like this, Madam President,” said Pak Suryo, chairman of one major coalition party, in a one-on-one meeting with Nisa one afternoon. “This 'Bold Spark' issue, frankly, is very easily twisted by political opponents into an ethnic/religious/racial issue or an attack on conservative values still strong in our society,” he continued carefully. “Maybe… maybe it's best that for now we focus more on communicating more 'concrete' economic programs whose impact is easier to measure for voters? So as not to keep giving free ammunition to the opposition.”

Nisa felt the political walls seeming to move closer, trying to squeeze her room to maneuver from all directions. And what made her feel more pressured was field reports showing the negative impact of this political storm beginning to be felt directly by the creators who should have been her program's main targets.

In Surabaya, Ibu Santi's struggle reached an increasingly critical point. No longer just anonymous mean comments on social media she faced. Now, she became the target of a far more structured and cruel black campaign. Articles appeared on several shady online news portals (which she suspected were funded by jealous business competitors or perhaps a party displeased with her association with the Palace program) accusing her rainbow layered cake business of using dangerous preservatives or even questioning its halal certification. Her beautiful product photos were negatively edited to look dull and unappealing. There was also a systematic effort to mass-give one-star ratings on her business's Google Maps page and online food ordering platforms, accompanied by fake damaging reviews.

The result was predictable: her sales revenue plunged drastically again. She tried fighting back with all her strength by making clarifications, showing halal certification evidence and lab tests of raw materials, helped by her daughter Anisa, her loyal customer community, and the crisis management mentoring team from the Creative Accelerator. However, the fight against structured slander felt so exhausting, draining her energy, emotions, and also her savings to their lowest point.

“It just doesn't feel worth it anymore, Nduk,” she complained to Anisa one night, her tears no longer held back seeing that day's sales report, completely empty. “Ma struggles honestly, makes delicious cake, but instead gets slandered this cruelly. Should Ma just close the business?”

In Yogyakarta, Maya the illustrator also felt a different but equally painful impact. After going through an intense inner struggle, she finally worked up the courage to send several key panels of her Roro Jonggrang digital comic version to her Accelerator program mentor. That mentor gave very high appreciation for the visual quality, cultural research detail, and depth of story Maya tried to raise. However, the mentor also, with good intentions, gave additional notes full of caution.

“The theme is very strong and relevant, Maya. Your visuals are also amazing,” the mentor wrote in her reply email. “But considering the sensitive political and social situation right now, after the Bima and Andi cases, maybe we need to reconsider how the gender issue is presented so it's not easily misinterpreted or considered an attack on certain cultural or religious values by less open-minded groups. We need a very mature visual and narrative communication strategy if a work this bold is to be published widely.”

That advice, actually well-intentioned and protective from the mentor, instead triggered a new storm of anxiety within Maya. Is my work really too dangerous? Too provocative? she thought. Am I ready to face a storm of criticism, personal attacks, or even threats like what happened to Bima, Andi, or even Ibu Santi? She again doubted continuing that dream project. She closed the Roro Jonggrang comic file tightly again on her laptop, buried under a new layer of doubt.

Bima in Jakarta, on the other side of the spectrum, began feeling frustrated with the direction of the mentoring process he was going through at the art studio. He felt his 'original voice,' raw and full of anger, was being tried to be 'tamed,' directed into something more 'polite' and 'safe' so as not to cause new controversy for the program. Offers to perform at several independent community music events, which he'd started getting regularly, now felt drastically reduced. Event organizers, though sympathetic to him, seemed afraid to take the risk of inviting him for fear their event would also be labeled controversial or even forcibly disbanded by opposing mass organizations. He felt trapped in a lose-lose position: attacked if too 'bold' voicing street reality, but ignored and considered 'having gone soft' if trying to be more 'safe' and poetic. He began questioning again his decision to get involved in the Palace program he'd originally hoped could give him a wider stage.

All these reports of pressure from outside and inside, and these bitter stories from creators in the field, ultimately flowed back to one person: President Nisa Farha. Her nights were again filled with piles of political risk analysis reports, negative news summaries, and internal memos containing whispers of doubt from her own circle of power. The deep exhaustion that had briefly vanished after successfully passing the Family Readiness Bill some months ago now felt like it was returning to plague her, perhaps even heavier, because this time it concerned the hopes and fragility of so many creative individuals she'd tried to push to be brave.

One night, well past midnight, Reza found her still lost in thought alone in her spacious but silent office. Nisa just sat quietly in her grand chair, staring blankly at the window showing the night's darkness, a cup of tea on her desk long gone cold, untouched. Nisa's face looked so pale and tired under the dim desk lamp's light.
“Not asleep yet, love?” Reza asked gently, walking slowly toward Nisa's desk, placing a fresh warm cup of tea he'd made beside Nisa's cold cup.

Nisa looked up slowly, trying to smile but failing. Her smile looked so forced and burdened. “So much to think about, Mas,” she answered quietly, her voice hoarse. Reza pulled up the guest chair, sitting facing Nisa. He reached for Nisa's hand, which felt cold. “I know all this has been very heavy lately,” he said softly, his gaze full of sympathy and worry. “Attacks coming from all directions. Pressure from within the coalition itself. On top of that, the creators we're trying to help end up becoming victims or even sources of new problems. I worry all this is draining your energy too much, Nisa.”

Nisa let out a long sigh, the heavy burden in her chest feeling so tight it was hard to breathe. She looked at Reza, her eyes now welling with tears ready to spill. “I… I'm starting to doubt, Mas,” she finally admitted that bitter honesty, her voice quiet, almost inaudible. “Have I been too naive all along? Too idealistic? Is this 'Bold Spark' idea really too utopian for our complicated political and social reality?”

Tears began pooling at the corners of her eyes. “I intended to give them wings to fly higher, but maybe… maybe I instead pushed them to fly too fast toward a storm without a strong enough shield.” Those tears finally fell, wetting her cheeks. “Seeing Ibu Santi attacked this cruelly just for trying to rise up… Seeing Maya afraid again and sinking into her anxiety… Seeing Bima frustrated and feeling betrayed… It feels… it feels like I've failed to protect them. Failed to keep my own promise.” A held-back sob escaped her lips.

Reza immediately rose from his chair, kneeling beside Nisa's chair, then took both his wife's hands, holding them tightly. “Nisa, listen to me,” he said gently but firmly, trying to pull Nisa from the pit of despair. “You haven't failed. Not at all.” He looked deep into his wife's eyes. “You're trying to do something very difficult, Nisa. Something perhaps never tried before by a leader on a scale this big: trying to change mindset, growing confidence and ethical responsibility at the same time. That's definitely a long process, definitely messy at the start, and there will definitely be inevitable casualties or negative side effects.”

He wiped the tears on Nisa's cheeks with his thumb. “But if we retreat now just because we're afraid of this storm,” he continued, “if we let opportunistic and cynical voices like Hardiman's win, if we stop this program just because there are a few problem cases at the start, what message do we send to millions of other creators out there who might still be keeping their dreams silently? The message we'd send is: 'Don't dare to dream. Don't dare to speak up. Stay in your safe and comfortable place of doubt.'”

Reza tightened his grip. “I'm not saying this is easy, love. I'm also angry and frustrated seeing what happened to Ibu Santi, Maya, and Bima,” he admitted honestly. “But we mustn't give up on our original vision just because there's a sharp rock in the road. Maybe the strategy needs adjusting. Maybe the mentoring needs strengthening. Maybe we need to focus more on raising success stories that truly embody the 'Guard the Values' spirit to balance the negative narrative. Strengthen the digital literacy and mental health mentoring modules more massively in the Accelerator. Fight hoaxes and slander like what happened to Ibu Santi more systematically, not just reactively. There are many ways to fix this, Nisa, without having to kill the flame.”

Reza's words, as usual, managed to become an anchor calming the storm in Nisa's heart. Not an instant solution he offered, but a new perspective, a reminder of their struggle's original purpose, and an injection of strength not to simply give up.

Nisa took a deep breath, trying to control her sobbing. “Yes,” she whispered quietly, wiping away her remaining tears. “You're right, Mas. We mustn't give up just because it's hard. But we do need a more mature new strategy.” That night, the two of them sat for a long time in Nisa's quiet office, no longer in tension or despair, but in intense strategic discussion. They remapped tactical steps to save the “Bold Spark” program without having to sacrifice its ideal vision. They realized the battle in Parliament over this program's budget in the upcoming General Hearing with Commission VIII, coming in a few weeks, would be a very crucial moment. They had to be able to present strong defensive data. Not only about abstract creative economy potential, but especially about the real qualitative impact on mindset change, on increasing creators' resilience, on inspiring stories like Ibu Santi, Maya, or Bima who managed to get through this initial storm.

Nisa ended that long night by sending a short message through an encrypted app to Angel and Anton: “Immediately prepare our strongest presentation materials for the Commission VIII hearing. Main focus on qualitative impact data, beneficiary testimonials showing resilience, and the urgency of long-term investment in brave and responsible creative human resources. I admit, the storm that came was stronger than we anticipated. But precisely because of that, this spark of responsible courage must be guarded together so it doesn't go out.”

The opportunistic echo from political opponents might grow louder. Whispers of doubt from the internal circle might grow more intense. However, in the heart of the Palace that night, the resolve to continue the “Bold Spark” struggle, though now with a more careful and measured strategy, was reaffirmed. The real battle for this movement's future was just about to enter a fiercer and more decisive chapter.
7: Istana Negara and Various Other Locations – Weeks and Months After the House Commission VIII Decision (Around Late 2046)

The House of Representatives Commission VIII's decision some weeks ago was like a double-edged sword for President Nisa Farha and the future of the National Movement “Bold Spark, Guard the Values.” On one hand, her cherished program survived the threat of total shutdown that had once felt so real amid the storm of the Bima and Andi scandals. But on the other hand, the 30 percent budget cut and the formation of an Independent Oversight Team recommended by the House became a new challenge no less complicated. The hardest political storm wind might have passed, but now Nisa and her team had to learn to 'dance' at the edge of a narrow budget cliff and under a potentially unfriendly oversight gaze.

The atmosphere in the Palace's Situation Room during the follow-up strategy meeting felt different. No more panic like during the Bima crisis, or anger like when the Andi scandal broke. What existed now was energy focused on adaptation, on how to maximize impact with more limited resources.

“We accept this House decision as a challenge, not as a defeat,” Nisa said, opening the meeting with a firm but calm tone, looking at her core team: Reza, Anton, Angel, and representatives from the Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy and the Ministry of Education. “Our priority now is no longer maximum quantity expansion, but deepening quality and strengthening the ethical foundation.”

Anton Prasetya immediately presented the budget-cut impact scenario he'd prepared. “With the 30 percent cut, Madam President, we're forced to make several significant adjustments,” he explained while showing slides full of numbers and graphs. “The target number of Spark Fund beneficiaries per batch has to be reduced by about 40 percent. However, we can make this a momentum to tighten the selection process. The main focus is no longer on mere virality potential, but on idea originality, research depth, long-term social or cultural impact potential, and especially, applicants' real commitment to the Guard the Values Charter.”

He continued, “For the Creative & Mental Accelerator, the frequency of bootcamp roadshows to major cities may have to be reduced. But, we can reallocate the budget to strengthen online modules to be more interactive and reach more creators in regions that have so far had minimal access. We also need to strengthen the portion of material on digital literacy, creative ethics, IP management, and techniques for facing cyberbullying, learning from last time's cases.”

“And for Bold Stage,” Anton added, “the plan to expand building physical creative hubs in several new provinces is forced to be postponed for now. However, all resources can be focused on building a Digital Bold Stage platform version 2.0 that's far more sophisticated, interactive, and well-integrated with the work curation system, content reporting, and learning modules.”

Reza Satria chimed in, reporting the results of his exploration with the private sector. “Good news, Nisa, friends in the private sector are actually more interested in getting involved after seeing your commitment to keep this program and your speech about collaboration,” he said. “One big technology group has already stated willingness to become the main partner developing that Bold Stage Digital 2.0 platform. Several other companies are ready to support online mentorship programs for Accelerator graduates or provide seed funding for Spark Fund projects considered most business-potential. So, the funding shortfall from the state budget can partly be covered from here.”

Nisa nodded, relieved hearing the news from Reza. “That's very good, Mas. Keep intensifying communication and collaboration with them,” she said. “Make this a truly mutual cooperation movement between government, private sector, and community.” She then turned to Angel. “Angel, our communication strategy also has to adapt. Echo this new narrative: focus on quality, integrity, and collaboration. Keep raising success stories that truly embody the 'Bold Responsibly' spirit. Show the public and the House that this program, though its budget is adjusted, still runs effectively and delivers real impact.”

That adaptation strategy was quickly executed. Nisa herself reappeared before the public through short live broadcasts and a special P3K podcast episode, transparently explaining the program's adjustments due to the budget decision, but framing it as a challenge to become more efficient, more quality-focused, and more collaborative. She again shared the inspiring stories of Ibu Santi's struggle and Maya's first steps, emphasizing that the spirit of “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” wasn't determined by budget size, but by its participants' resilience and integrity.

However, a new challenge soon emerged from an already-anticipated direction: the Independent Oversight Team. Following the House's recommendation, this team was finally formed. Its composition, as Nisa and Reza feared, was a problematic mix. There were indeed several communication academics and legal experts with good, independent reputations, plus representatives from civil society organizations focused on digital literacy. However, also seated within it were two names publicly known to have affiliation, or at least political views, opposed to Nisa, including Dr. Alif, a conservative sociologist who often criticized Nisa's previous policies. Their presence was clearly a political maneuver from Hardiman's camp to 'lock in' and look for faults in the program from within.

The first meeting between the Program Implementation Team (represented by Anton and Angel) and the Oversight Team took place in a neutral meeting room at the State Secretariat office, its atmosphere feeling formal and very stiff. After introductions and a brief presentation from Anton about the program's achievements so far and the adaptation strategy after the budget adjustment, the Q&A session began. Professor Amir, a communications academic appointed as team chair, asked relatively constructive questions about the Bold Stage curation mechanism and the Mental Accelerator's impact evaluation. But when it was Dr. Alif's turn to speak, the atmosphere changed instantly.

“I want to go back to the Bima and Andi cases that caused such an uproar,” said Dr. Alif, his voice flat but full of scrutiny. “We from the Oversight Team need full access to all minutes of the psychological mentoring sessions given to Mr. Bima. We also need to see the complete data of the initial selection process that could let through a plagiarist creator's proposal like Andi Saputra, whom you even promoted as a success example.”

Anton calmly explained that mentoring session minutes were confidential because they concerned personal counseling aspects between creator and psychologist, but they could provide an anonymous summary report on progress. Regarding Andi, Anton again acknowledged the weakness in the initial plagiarism detection system, now significantly improved, and asserted that support had been withdrawn immediately after the case broke, in line with accountability principles.

But Dr. Alif seemed unsatisfied. “We need full transparency, Mr. Anton, not an anonymous summary,” he pressed. “How can the public trust this program is accountable if important data is instead concealed from the oversight team formed by the House?” He then moved to questions about the Guard the Values Charter. “This charter sounds good on paper. But what's its concrete implementation in the field? Who has the right to determine a work violates 'values'? Is there a double standard in its application? Let's not have this charter become just lip service or a tool to silence criticism the Palace dislikes, while works that are disturbing or violate ethics keep being allowed to circulate in the name of 'courage.'”

The questions from Dr. Alif and other oversight team members who shared his views clearly implied deep distrust and intent to find fault however small. That first meeting ended with a long list of data and document requests to be prepared by Anton and Angel's team in a short time, plus a schedule of intense routine meetings every two weeks. Clearly, this Oversight Team would become a new 'thorn in the flesh' for the program's implementation.

Anton and Angel reported the results of that meeting to Nisa in a worried tone. “They clearly didn't come as an oversight partner wanting to help improvement, Madam,” Angel said frankly. “The direction of their questions was very cornering and tendentious. It felt like undergoing an investigative audit by the Supreme Audit Agency or the Anti-Corruption Commission, not ordinary program monitoring.”

Nisa sighed, but her face showed she'd already anticipated this would happen. “I figured,” she said quietly. “Hardiman and friends won't stay silent after failing to stop this program at the budget meeting. They'll use this Oversight Team as a new tool to disrupt us from within, looking for gaps to attack again.” She looked at Anton and Angel in turn. “My instruction is clear: Serve all their reasonable data requests in line with applicable confidentiality rules,” she asserted. “Keep our process transparent. But don't let them intimidate you or try to intervene in the program's substance and the creative process currently running.” She added, “We have to be neater, more meticulous in every documentation and reporting from now on. This will certainly add to your workload, will be very exhausting, but let's face this new challenge professionally.”

The undercurrent of tight oversight and potential bureaucratic intervention now became a new reality Nisa and her team had to face every day in running “Bold Spark, Guard the Values.” However, amid the budget adaptation challenge and new oversight pressure, a glimmer of light actually began to emerge from the creators themselves. The fruit of their resilience, the result of the mentoring process that kept running despite limited resources, began to be harvested. The first good news came from Yogyakarta. After weeks of anxiously waiting following a tense virtual presentation, an English-language email arrived in Maya's inbox. Her heart pounded hard opening it. Her work, the initial panels of the Roro Jonggrang digital comic, passed final selection and was named one of ten finalists in the Southeast Asian Digital Comic Competition! An extraordinary achievement for a young illustrator who months ago was still sinking in self-doubt. More than that, as a finalist, she not only received development prize money, but also the chance for her work to be exhibited in an international virtual gallery and noticed by renowned comic editors and publishers from various countries serving as judges. Her courage to submit her work, her courage to face her biggest fear, was now bearing unexpected sweet fruit.

In Jakarta, Bima finally released his new song, “Voice in the Dark Alley,” independently through the Bold Stage digital channel and several alternative music streaming platforms. Its release was done without great fanfare, just a simple announcement from his art studio and a few community friends. The public reaction this time was indeed very different compared to when “Rats in Neckties” exploded. No overnight viral explosion, but also no mass condemnation or controversy accompanying it. What emerged instead was more substantive discussion and critical appreciation. Independent music observers praised Bima's maturity in writing lyrics that remained sharp but were more poetic and reflective, and his music arrangement that was more mature and rich in nuance. Social activists appreciated his message that still voiced the marginalized's unease but in a way that invited thought, not just provoking anger. Several community media outlets and independent music blogs reviewed it positively. Of course, some of his old fans still missed Bima's old 'fierceness,' or considered him to have 'gone soft' and lost his bite. But Bima himself, reading the more varied comments and deeper discussion about his song, felt more at peace. He felt his message this time landed in a different way, a way perhaps not explosive, but more absorbing and thought-provoking. He began understanding that the courage to speak didn't always have to mean shouting the loudest or using the crudest language. He sent a short message to his mentor at the studio: “Thanks for being so patient dealing with a stubborn head like me, man. Seems like… seems like I'm starting to find the right way for my voice now.”

The most joyful news perhaps came from Surabaya. At the Surabaya District Court, after several fairly exhausting continued hearings, the judge finally read the verdict on the shop eviction lawsuit filed by the shop owner against Ibu Santi. The result: the lawsuit was rejected! The judge deemed the reason of 'residents' complaints about public order disturbance' filed by the shop owner's side unfounded and unsupported by strong evidence. Conversely, evidence of support from Ibu Santi's loyal customer community, the viral online petition #JagaKueIbuSanti, and the defense from the legal aid team assisting her (facilitated by the Accelerator network) became important considerations for the judge in deciding the case. This victory was welcomed with tearful cheers by Anisa and Ibu Santi's supporters who faithfully accompanied her at every hearing. More than just keeping her kitchen's stove burning, this was a symbolic victory against intimidation, slander, and attempts to obstruct a small business trying to rise. News of Ibu Santi's legal victory went viral again, this time with a positive narrative about the power of community solidarity and the importance of integrity in doing business amid sometimes cruel competition. Her cake business slowly rose again, even stronger than before because of the positive publicity and moral support she received. She became real proof that the resilience the Mental Accelerator program tried to build could truly bear fruit.

Nisa and Reza received this good news about Maya's brave step breaking into the international arena, about Bima's new, more mature and meaningful song, and about Ibu Santi's inspiring legal victory with relieved smiles and deep gratitude at the Palace. Amid political pressure from the Oversight Team and existing budget constraints, these real stories from the field became new fuel, strengthening their spirit to keep continuing the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” program.

“See, Mas?” Nisa said to Reza one night, showing the news of Ibu Santi's victory on her tablet. “In the end, this isn't just about percentage figures in the budget. It's not about how many views or likes. It's about them.” She looked at Reza. “About one Maya in Jogja who finally dared to submit her work to the Southeast Asian level after years trapped in fear. About one Ibu Santi in Surabaya whose kitchen wasn't evicted because of the strength of mutual solidarity. About one Bima in Jakarta who's starting to find a wiser way to speak up without having to lose his idealism.”
