Reza smiled, hugging his wife. “I know, love,” he answered gently. “And these are the stories we must keep raising and echoing continuously. This is our best ammunition against anyone trying to belittle or stop this program.”

Though they knew the challenges ahead were still big — especially facing the scrutinizing Oversight Team and potential further intervention — that night, Nisa and Reza could sleep a little more soundly. The seeds of courage they'd planted, though growing slowly and having to pass through various storms, began showing real results on their creators' personal stages. Hope, though it had once dimmed, now burned brighter again, fueled by stories of resilience from the grassroots.
8: Moving Forward
Istana Negara and the Indonesian Landscape – Spring 2046, About a Year After the “Bold Spark” Political Storm Subsided

A spring breeze blew gently across Istana Negara's neatly kept back garden, carrying the fresh scent of flamboyant flowers just blooming after last night's rain. Jakarta's sky, for a moment, looked clear blue without the usual suffocating pollution, as if reflecting a political atmosphere relatively calmer than a year ago. The great controversy storm that struck the National Movement “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” had subsided, replaced by a more stable work rhythm, more focused on deepening quality and upholding ethical principles that were now the new mantra.

In one shady corner of the garden, under the shelter of an old trembesi tree that had silently witnessed many historical events, a simple but meaningful event was underway: the launch of the Digital Bold Stage platform version 2.0. No excessive luxury like the movement's initial launch. Just a few large monitor screens displaying the platform's new, now more interactive and secure interface, a few small booths showcasing the latest works of mentored creators — this time with strong emphasis on narratives of originality, social impact, and ethical creative process — and dozens of more carefully selected guests: young creators who were finalists of the latest Spark Fund cohort, representatives of major digital platforms now partners, several communication and law academics, members of the Independent Oversight Team whose presence was a constant reminder of accountability, and of course, the Palace's core team.

President Nisa Farha and Reza Satria stood in the front row, carefully listening to Anton Prasetya's presentation about the platform's new features. Anton explained the interactive digital literacy and creative ethics module now a mandatory requirement for all Spark Fund recipients; the problematic content reporting system (hoaxes, plagiarism, bullying) now directly integrated with the Communications Ministry's Anti-Hoax Task Force and Police systems; and the work curation mechanism for monthly showcases now involving an independent expert panel from various disciplines alongside the Palace's internal team, for the sake of objectivity and quality. This platform was the real embodiment of the bitter but necessary evolution of the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” campaign — an adaptive response born from the crisis that had nearly sunk the entire program a year ago.

Nisa smiled thinly seeing from a distance the enthusiasm of several young creators trying the interactive module demo on copyright and proper citation techniques at one booth. A warm relief spread through her heart, but also a deep awareness of the long, winding, wound-filled journey they'd taken together to reach this point. Her gaze briefly met Reza's beside her, a look full of understanding and shared history passing between them without needing words. This new platform launch wasn't just a technology ceremony, but an important moment for reflection: about the storm that had passed and the new direction the compass was now heading.

An expensive lesson, Nisa thought to herself, while listening to remarks from a representative of one major digital platform now sounding far more cooperative than before. Her mind unconsciously drifted back to the darkest times a year ago, when her dream program nearly shattered completely. She remembered the tremor in her hands the first time she saw evidence of Andi Saputra's plagiarism, the new idol creator who turned out to have stolen others' work; the betrayal that felt so personal yet also political, because she'd praised Andi openly. She remembered her overflowing anger and frustration seeing Bima's song lyrics so carelessly touching on ethnic/religious issues and sparking flames of division; and the painful dilemma when she had to draw an ethical line that got her accused of silencing freedom of expression by some circles. The shadow of the cruel doxing case against Cantika Ayu, the beauty tutorial creator, still left wounds and guilt in her heart — a tragic reminder of how her good intent to push courage could be misconstrued as license to hurt if not accompanied by solid ethical fences and digital understanding.

She remembered the long sleepless nights at the crisis's peak, political pressure from all directions, the illegal campaign fund slander that attacked her integrity to the bone, and perhaps most painful of all, the rift that once felt so real in her relationship with Reza, her last line of defense. That cold, despairing moment on the Palace balcony at dawn, when she felt so alone and nearly gave up on everything, still felt chillingly cold down her spine even now.

I was so naive back then, Nisa admitted to herself bitterly. Too burned up by idealism, too trusting in the power of good intent alone, forgetting to see the real battlefield's complexity. She thought that igniting the spark of courage alone was enough to burn away the inferior mentality and collective doubt that had long confined the nation's creative potential. She forgot, a fire lit without control and clear direction could consume the house of hope she was building. She forgot that courage without responsibility is destructive anarchy. That freedom without ethics is painful arbitrariness.

However, it was precisely amid that darkest storm that she also found unexpected strengths that saved her. Strength from Reza's unconditional support, standing firmly by her side even at her lowest point. Strength from quiet but brave voices like “Sarah's,” emerging from the grassroots at the most critical moment, reminding her again of her struggle's purpose. Strength from her core team's unwavering solidity — Anton who stayed analytical seeking solutions, Angel who tough-mindedly managed the communication crisis, Adam who calmly deflected media attacks. And strength from the public's resurgence, which turned out not easily fooled by slander, rising to give moral support through the hashtag #SayaBersamaPresidenNisa (#IStandWithPresidentNisa) when she needed it most. That wave of solidarity gave her reason to rise from despair and keep fighting.

The political victory in rejecting the special committee proposal on “Bold Spark” in the House was indeed strategically relieving. But Nisa fully realized, the most valuable lesson from this whole dark episode wasn't about winning or losing in political maneuvering. The most important lesson was about the process of learning and adapting as a leader, and also as a human being. About the importance of having the humility to acknowledge mistakes or shortcomings in our policies. About the courage to change strategic direction when needed, even if it means admitting our initial approach was flawed. And about the steadfastness to keep holding core principles — in this case integrity and responsibility — even while facing storm pressure from all directions. She learned that true leadership isn't about maintaining popularity or pleasing everyone, but about the courage to make hard decisions believed right for long-term good, even having to pay the expensive price of criticism, attacks, or even losing some support.

Nisa's daydream broke when the platform launch event ended and the invited guests began moving to enjoy light refreshments provided in the garden tent. Reza approached, touching her arm gently. “Daydreaming far away, Madam President?” he teased with a smile.

Nisa smiled back. “Just a little reflection,” she answered. They walked together, moving slightly away from the crowd, toward a quieter corner of the garden. “This new platform looks promising,” Reza said, opening the conversation, breaking the comfortable silence between them. “The integration between Bold Stage content and the digital literacy module and reporting system is a very right strategic step, Nisa. Learning from last time's bitter experience.”

“Yes,” Nisa nodded in agreement. “Conceptually and technologically, I'm quite satisfied. But the biggest challenge later will be in implementation and consistency.” She looked at Reza. “Making sure that digital literacy module really changes creators' mindset and behavior, not just a formal green-checkmark to get the Spark Fund. Making sure the Anti-Hoax Task Force and the platform's internal team are truly responsive in following up on problematic content reports fairly and quickly, not just moving when there's public pressure or a viral case.” She sighed. “Building a healthy digital ethics culture in this country is a decades-long marathon job, Mas, not a one-or-two-year program sprint.”

“At least we've started that marathon with the right steps now, Nisa,” Reza replied, holding his wife's hand. He smiled remembering the past. “I still remember how chaotic our situation was a year ago when the Andi scandal exploded. It felt like the whole foundation of the program we'd just built collapsed instantly. The two of us almost collapsed with it too.”

“I remember,” Nisa replied quietly, her voice a bit hoarse recalling that difficult time. “I remember how afraid and desperate I was then. Afraid of failing totally, afraid of disappointing everyone who'd trusted me, afraid… of losing your support.” That confession came out just like that, honest and fragile, a side she only showed to Reza.

Reza tightened his grip. “We almost lost our own directions then, didn't we?” he continued. “I also wavered and doubted for a moment. The pressure from Hadi Kusuma's circle and the business network over the Sarah Wijaya book issue made me briefly blind to the right priorities.” He looked closely at Nisa, his eyes conveying both regret and lesson-learning. “But seeing you stay firm on principle, daring to take the risk of supporting Sarah even knowing it would complicate your political position and mine too… seeing you rise again with your head held high after being hit by that campaign fund slander… all of that reawakened me to what's truly important in this life. Not just business connections or false political stability. But integrity. Honesty to conscience.”

“And seeing you finally take a firm stance about Hadi, choosing truth over old friendship… seeing you stand by me unconditionally when I felt darkest and most alone… that gave me more strength than anything, Mas,” Nisa returned Reza's gaze, her eyes now welling with emotion. “We really learned so much about ourselves, and especially about the strength of our relationship, during that tremendous storm.”

“Yes,” Reza smiled gently, stroking the back of Nisa's hand. “We learned again that the openness and honesty we prided ourselves on at the start of our marriage must be continuously tested and renewed in every life phase. That being a true partner isn't just about sharing laughter in good times, but especially about having to be each other's anchor in the fiercest storms. About having to remind each other when one starts to waver, strengthen each other when the other is fragile, even having to forgive each other if unintentionally hurting one another due to pressure.”

They fell silent for a moment, absorbing the deep meaning of their intertwined marriage and leadership journey. Scars from yesterday's storm might not be visible physically, but both knew, the bond between them now felt far stronger, more mature, forged by the fire of the heaviest trial.

Amid that garden's calm, Nisa again remembered the ripples of problems still remaining. “But our work isn't done, Mas,” she whispered, returning to reality. “Resistance from old groups might just be sleeping briefly, waiting for a chance to rise again. The political opposition group, though failing with the special committee, will surely keep looking for new gaps to attack our policies in other areas. The 'absolute freedom' creator groups also still often voice criticism on alternative platforms, accusing us of covert censorship. And at the grassroots,” she sighed, “debate about the Family Readiness Bill's implementation, about the line between tradition, religion, and individual rights, I hear is still ongoing intensely in many regions. Social and cultural change is indeed a very long process that's never truly finished.”

Indonesia's creative and digital landscape had indeed changed subtly but significantly since “Bold Spark” was rolled out with all its drama. Public discussion about digital ethics, copyright, hoax dangers, and cancel culture was now far more lively and deep. Universities began including courses on digital media ethics. Mainstream mass media, though still trapped in click wars, now looked a little more careful in reporting sensitive issues and more often did verification. Major digital platforms, pushed by firmer regulation and public demand driven by the Palace, began improving their content moderation systems and reporting features, though results were still far from ideal. Awareness of the importance of originality, fact verification, and social impact of work among creators themselves also felt increased. Many new communities emerged focused on “positive content” or “ethical creativity.” Of course, sensation-chasing creators and unhealthy competition still abounded. Small controversy ripples still often emerged. But at least, now there was a stronger counter-narrative, an ethical standard beginning to be jointly referenced (the Guard the Values Charter), and clearer consequences for violations. The Independent Oversight Team also kept running its function, becoming a 'whip' reminder for the government to keep the creator empowerment program accountable and not deviate from its original purpose, ensuring the emphasis on ethics didn't turn into covert censorship. “So, what's our next step now, Madam President?” Reza asked with a slightly formal tone but full of smiles, pulling Nisa back from her reflective daydream, returning focus to the future.

Nisa smiled, holding her husband's hand more tightly. “The next step is to keep working hard and consistently, Mas,” she answered firmly. “Making sure this Bold Stage 2.0 platform truly functions optimally and safely for creators. Overseeing the Family Readiness Bill's implementation in the regions with a wise and persuasive approach, not forcing. Continuing to open space for dialogue with all parties, including those still resistant.”

She paused briefly, looking into Reza's eyes. “And most important of all,” she continued quietly, “is to keep learning from every process, from every mistake, from every success.” She looked toward the dusk sky now starting to turn dark, decorated with the first twinkling stars. “We might never be able to create a perfect, flawless creativity paradise in this country,” she murmured. “But we can, and must, keep trying to build a more just, more ethical, and more humane ecosystem.” She continued, as if reformulating her struggle's vision. “An ecosystem where the courage to speak up and create is always balanced with the courage to take responsibility. Where every spark of creativity can become a guiding light for the nation's progress, rather than becoming embers that burn down our own house.”

Slowly, they walked back hand in hand toward the Palace building, now lit by night lamps, leaving the garden that was starting to empty. No more doubt shadowing their steps, only calm resolve and deep understanding of the immense complexity of the task they bore as the nation's leaders. They realized, this journey was an endless journey to keep balancing burning idealism with often bitter reality; between pushing fast change and wisely managing its impact; between lighting the flame of hope without having to burn the bridges of dialogue.

This nation's compass might have found a new direction that felt more balanced between courage and responsibility. But that compass would keep moving, keep seeking a dynamic equilibrium point amid the ripples of an era that never stopped churning. And Nisa Farha, together with Reza Satria always faithfully by her side, was ready to keep guiding that long journey. With a heart now wiser from being forged by storms, a soul stronger from trials, and love for this country that never diminished in the slightest. The light of hope after the storm now felt not just warmly calming, but also became a torch illuminating the long, challenging road ahead of them.

However, Nisa hadn't yet fully realized, a new, more fundamental challenge, one that would test the very main pillar of the rule of law itself, was peeking from behind this curtain of false calm, waiting for its time to surface.
9: Istana Negara, Jakarta and Various Corners of Indonesia – Early 2048

Jakarta's sky was clear blue that morning, refracting a false hope with its calm that seemed untouched by the noisy metropolitan pulse of life racing below. Inside the cool and silent Presidential Working Room, Nisa Farha had just finished a brief virtual meeting with several governors from eastern Indonesia, discussing progress on social aid distribution after a small natural disaster struck Nusa Tenggara a few weeks ago.

More than two years had passed since the last political storm that tested the resilience of the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” program to its lowest point. Now, that program ran with a breath that felt more regulated, more mature, and more careful. Its focus had shifted from merely igniting the spark of courage to balancing it with enforcing ethics and responsibility, an expensive lesson learned from various earlier controversies. Likewise with the Family Readiness Bill; its implementation kept rolling under the tight supervision of the National Population and Family Planning Board and the Ministry of Women's Empowerment. Initial reports from several pilot regions showed positive trends, though slow, in declining early marriage rates and significant increase in public access to premarital family counseling.

A rare flicker of satisfaction settled briefly in Nisa's heart as she signed the final approval sheet on her always-neat and organized mahogany work desk. A warm cup of jasmine tea — her morning ritual that never changed since she took office — stood faithfully beside her, spreading a gentle, calming scent, contrasting with the smell of document paper and the cold air conditioning. For a moment, she felt like a captain who had finally managed to steer her ship through two great consecutive storms — the Family Bill storm and the Bold Spark storm. The political ocean might not be entirely calm, there were still small ripples from the opposition and undercurrents of resistance to change that needed continued watching, but at least this big ship called Indonesia kept sailing forward, even with a compass direction that felt more solid toward the Golden Indonesia 2050 vision she always dreamed of.

However, that morning calm was instantly disturbed when her office door was knocked gently and Angel Marina entered, carrying a cream-colored folder Nisa recognized as the folder for urgent reports or sensitive issues needing her immediate attention. Her trusted assistant's face looked different from usual; the efficient smile always decorating her face was now replaced by a line of seriousness and concern that couldn't be hidden. “Good morning, Madam President,” Angel greeted, her voice sounding a bit quieter than usual. “Sorry to disturb your quiet time. There's a report and an audience request letter that just came in this morning from the Mitra Legal Aid Institute advocacy team in Palu, Central Sulawesi. I think you need to see this right away.”

Nisa's brow furrowed. LBH Central Sulawesi? Her feeling started to turn uneasy. She took that cream folder from Angel's hand. Inside, attached was a neat legal case summary, several news clippings from local Palu newspapers, and a handwritten audience request letter with trembling but neat writing, implying a deep despair. The name of that audience requester struck straight into Nisa's memory: Siti Rahayu.

That name brought Nisa back to the early days of the Family Readiness Bill struggle. She remembered once briefly reading news about Siti a few months after the law was passed, in the daily media report Angel prepared. Siti's story then was a moving early success story from that new law's implementation. A 19-year-old village girl from a simple family in inland Central Sulawesi, smart and highly aspiring to become an elementary school teacher, forced by her family to accept a marriage proposal from a village head much older than her, a wealthy widower with strong political and economic influence in their sub-district area. Siti, who turned out to secretly often listen to socialization about the new Family Law from community radio broadcasts in her village, worked up the courage to reject that arranged marriage. With help from a BKKBN field extension officer and mentoring from LBH Mitra in Palu, she filed a petition to cancel the planned marriage with the local Religious Court. With great difficulty, through the mental and financial readiness assessment process mandated by the new law (which Siti clearly didn't meet, still fully dependent on her family and mentally unready to marry), plus evidence of coercion, that marriage was finally successfully canceled by the Religious Court's panel of judges. A small but brave victory against tradition and local power, a victory Nisa had once marked as good news strengthening her conviction about the positive impact of the law she fought for.

However, the report in her hands now told the next chapter of Siti Rahayu's story, a chapter far darker and more brutal. The village head, furious that his proposal was rejected and feeling his dignity as a respected figure trampled by an ordinary village girl, turned out not to stay silent. He launched a counterattack. Not only suing Siti and her family back at the District Court for defamation for rejecting his proposal, but also absurdly demanding compensation for all preparation costs for the proposal and the 'failed' marriage plan. Worse still, exploiting his influence and power over village officials and the local Land Agency, he suddenly sued for ownership of most of Siti's family's only inherited land, on the pretext of a land boundary dispute that had never existed before in decades.

The report from LBH Mitra attached the chronology of the land dispute trial at the local District Court that made Nisa's blood boil. The presiding judge leading the trial clearly sided with the influential village head from the start. Key witnesses from Siti's side trying to explain the land ownership history were often interrupted or their testimony deemed irrelevant by the judge. Land certificate evidence and old land deeds submitted by Siti's family as legitimate ownership proof were ignored on very contrived formal juridical-technical grounds. Conversely, testimony from several village officials subordinate to the village head, clearly giving false statements about land boundaries, was accepted just like that by the judge without further verification. The trial's final result was predictable: Siti and her family lost decisively. They not only lost most of their land, their only livelihood source, but were also threatened with having to pay case costs and 'immaterial damages' to the village head, in an amount impossible for them to fulfill in their lifetime. Their appeal effort also failed at the High Court on similar grounds. This audience request letter to the President was their last hope.

Nisa's breath caught after finishing reading that report. A freezing cold anger began spreading through her bloodstream. This was no longer just an ordinary legal dispute case between citizens. This was a brutal, naked portrait of how law, which should be a protective shield for the weak, a new law she'd fought for tooth and nail with all its political risk, could easily be paralyzed, even twisted into a weapon to destroy the victim, by corrupt local power forces and a broken judicial system. Siti's legal victory at the Religious Court some months ago seemed to mean nothing when facing the bitter reality at the District Court, which turned out could be 'arranged' by money and influence. The Family Readiness Bill she was proud of turned out to be nothing more than a paper shield easily torn by the sharp fangs of systemic injustice.
“Does Anton already know the details of this case's development?” Nisa asked quietly, her voice sounding flat, holding back the turmoil in her chest.

“Yes, Madam. I forwarded this LBH report to Mr. Anton last night,” Angel answered quietly. “Mr. Anton is asking his team at the Special Staff to conduct independent verification in Palu and find out more about the track record of the District Court judge handling this case. But from initial indications and this very detailed LBH report, there's strong suspicion of judicial mafia practice and legal manipulation involving local officials.”

Nisa closed that cream folder with a heavy hand movement. Siti Rahayu's shyly smiling but hopeful face in the small black-and-white photo attached to the LBH report — the smile of a young girl who felt she'd just won her first fight against bad fate — appeared so clearly in her mind. That hope had now been forcibly seized, replaced by a despair perhaps far darker.

Before the tightness in her chest from thinking about Siti Rahayu's tragic fate could subside, a short message notification from Anton Prasetya appeared on Nisa's tablet screen lying on the desk. That message contained a link to a news article from an independent local investigative journalism portal in West Kalimantan, accompanied by a short note from Anton: “Morning, Madam President. Permission to report a worrying development regarding the case of Dito Nugraha, an alumnus of the second cohort of 'Bold Spark' workshops in Pontianak. Related to potential abuse of the Electronic Information and Transactions Law.”

With an increasingly uneasy feeling, Nisa opened that news link. The main headline on that portal's page was enough to make her let out a long, heavy sigh: “After Exposing Alleged Illegal Gold Mine Extortion, Young Journalist Environmental Activist Charged with Defamation Under the Electronic Information Law.”

That article told in detail the story of Dito Nugraha, a 23-year-old Dayak youth, a recent journalism graduate from a local university who had just returned to his hometown in inland West Kalimantan. Dito was depicted as an idealistic figure with high enthusiasm after joining the “Ethical Investigative Journalism for Public Interest” workshop, part of the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” Creative & Mental Accelerator program a few months earlier. With the characteristic courage of a newly enlightened young person, Dito conducted a deep investigation alone into small-scale illegal gold mining practices (PETI) rampant and damaging the environment around his village. Through field tracing and secret interviews with several uneasy residents, Dito managed to gather evidence of village officials' involvement in smoothing that illegal mining operation, as well as strong suspicion of a routine flow of illegal levy funds from miners to an official at the local sub-district office as 'hush money.' His report, which he published as a long article with photographic evidence of damaged environmental conditions and interview recordings (with sources' voices disguised for safety) on his personal blog, later quoted by several small local media outlets in Pontianak, was written very carefully, trying to apply the investigative journalism principles he'd learned. He even explicitly cited the “Guard the Values” principle from the Bold Spark program in his article's introduction, emphasizing that his purpose was purely to uncover truth for public interest and environmental preservation, not to personally attack anyone.

However, his courage to voice the truth instead bore disaster. The sub-district official whose name was mentioned by initials in Dito's investigative report was furiously enraged. Instead of providing clarification or refuting the accusation with counter data and facts, he immediately took a shortcut: reporting Dito Nugraha to the local Police Precinct with a defamation accusation via electronic media, using a rubber clause in the Electronic Information and Transactions Law (UU ITE).

The legal process against Dito moved lightning fast, very contrasting with the slowness of handling other cases. The local District Prosecutor's Office, suspected of being pressured by that influential sub-district official, without conducting significant evidence deepening from Dito's side or proper digital forensic testing, immediately named Dito a suspect. Not long after, his case was quickly transferred to the District Court for trial. That news article also included interview quotes with Dito's lawyer from the local LBH, complaining how difficult it was for them to bring forward key witnesses who could ease Dito's case due to suspected intimidation from certain parties. That lawyer also highlighted how the judge trying this case seemed to ignore press law principles and evidence standards that should apply in cases related to journalistic work or the Electronic Information Law. Dito, the idealistic young journalist, now faced threat of prison just for daring to write the truth. Nisa massaged her temples, throbbing increasingly hard. The same pattern again, she thought bitterly. The courage she tried to ignite through the “Bold Spark” program. The courage to voice truth, to conduct social control, even having tried to apply the “Guard the Values” ethical principles. Instead cruelly broken by law enforcement officials suspected of colluding with corrupt local power. The Electronic Information Law, a legal product she'd ironically also supported revising to better protect citizens from cybercrime, was now so easily abused as an ultimate weapon to silence criticism, to criminalize citizen journalism, to protect corrupt officials. The spirit of “Courage” and “Guard the Values” she tried to instill through that empowerment program seemed powerless, crushed facing the thick wall of a legal system that turned out so easily manipulated.

“Ask Anton to also prepare a complete report and deep legal analysis on this Dito case, Angel,” Nisa ordered quietly, her voice sounding tired but firm. “And immediately coordinate with the Palace's legal team. Study the possibility we could provide legal protection or advocacy assistance for Dito, of course as far as allowed by rules and without appearing to directly intervene in the legal process.”

“Yes, Madam President. We'll carry that out right away,” Angel replied quietly, then excused herself out of the room carrying Siti Rahayu's case folder, leaving Nisa alone with her now fiercely churning thoughts.

These two cases — Siti Rahayu in Sulawesi and Dito Nugraha in Kalimantan — felt like a death bell for her naive optimism all this time. This was no longer just a casuistic incident, this was a symptom of a far more severe chronic disease within this country's law enforcement body. Nisa remembered again the sporadic complaints she sometimes heard in dialogue sessions during work visits to regions, or that she read from hundreds of citizen letters coming to the Palace every week. Stories about drawn-out legal processes without certainty. About case costs and 'grease money' choking ordinary people. About judges' verdicts that felt so odd and unjust. About the difficulty of accessing lawyers for those who couldn't afford them.

All this time, she might have focused too much on making new populist policies or fixing sectoral issues whose impact was more visibly apparent. She might have been too naive assuming the legal and judicial system would run on its own along the constitutional track, that partial reform in a few institutions was enough. But now she realized. That assumption was very wrong. The echo of injustice she heard so loudly from Sulawesi and Kalimantan this morning had opened her eyes wide. This rule-of-law nation's foundation turned out fragile. Very fragile.

Right as that bitter reflection reached its peak, her office door was knocked again. Anton Prasetya entered, this time not carrying a new gloomy case folder, but a tablet displaying a brief presentation slide full of data and graphs.

“Sorry to disturb again, Madam President,” Anton said. “But this might be relevant to what you're thinking about. Following your instruction some time ago to start specifically monitoring the performance indicators of our law enforcement institutions, this is a summary of the latest quarter's data we just compiled.”

Nisa invited Anton to sit and display his data on the large screen on her office wall. Anton began presenting his team's findings. Those cold numbers seemed to become a brutal confirmation of Nisa's bad premonition.

Corruption Perception Index (Judicial Sector): Indonesia's score still stagnant at 38, even dropping slightly 0.5 points compared to the previous year. Placing Indonesia at a worrying rank regionally, even below several neighboring countries once considered more corrupt. Internal surveys among business associations also still showed high complaints about 'unofficial' costs for handling legal cases or getting verdict 'certainty.'

Case Resolution Time: The average resolution time for ordinary civil cases at first-instance District Courts nationally increased 15% in the last two years, far exceeding the Supreme Court's standard operating procedure targets. Case backlog (cases undecided beyond the set time limit) reached the highest record in the last five years, especially for land dispute and labor dispute cases involving ordinary people against big corporations or local governments.

Public Trust in Legal Institutions: The latest National Survey conducted by an independent survey institute showed public trust levels in the Police, Prosecutor's Office, and Supreme Court institutions generally below 50 percent. The lowest trust came from respondents in low-income groups and those living outside Java Island. Quotes from qualitative survey results showed such bitter general sentiment: “Law in this country is sharp downward but blunt upward,” or “If you don't have a lot of money or strong backing, never hope to win in court against them.”

Access to Legal Aid: Data from the Ministry of Law and Human Rights showed state budget for accredited Legal Aid Institutes (LBH) and Legal Aid Posts (Posbakum) in courts indeed increased in recent years. However, its absorption was still low and its service reach still very limited. Many regencies/cities, especially outside Java, still didn't have an active accredited LBH providing free legal assistance for poor citizens.

Anton finished his presentation with a serious face, letting the data speak for itself. “Overall, Madam President,” he concluded, “this data, combined with cases like what happened to Ms. Siti Rahayu or Mr. Dito Nugraha, shows a very serious structural and systemic problem in our law enforcement machine. Partial reform or sectoral programs in each institution might no longer be effective enough. We need a policy breakthrough at a more fundamental level if we want the ideal of legal supremacy to truly materialize in this country, not just remain a slogan.”

Nisa stared blankly at the rows of numbers and graphs displayed on the large screen before her. Siti's case. Dito's case. Now reinforced by brutal and undeniable national statistical data. Doubt could no longer remain in her mind. This rule-of-law nation's foundation, which should be democracy and justice's main pillar in this country, was indeed fragile. Very fragile. All her hard work so far — pushing a fairer Family Law, igniting the spark of responsible creative courage — felt futile, felt like it would be in vain, if in the end the last fortress where citizens sought justice instead became the newest, most painful source of injustice.

How could a nation truly be free in soul and body if its own law could still be bought and sold or ignored by its officials? That fundamental question echoed so strongly in her mind, demanding an answer, demanding action. The fatigue from previous political battles seemed to vanish instantly, replaced by a wave of new energy that felt so strong — the energy of righteous anger over injustice, the energy of steel resolve to fix it from its roots, however great the risk ahead. She knew, the next battlefield had spread out before her. The most fundamental, most dangerous, but also most important battlefield for Indonesia's future.
10: The President's Working Room, Istana Negara – The Next Morning, 7:00 AM. Jakarta's morning air, usually already feeling warm with the pulse of activity and pollution, felt cool tending to cold inside the Presidential Working Room. The air conditioner worked silently, but couldn't cool the room's atmosphere, which since dawn had felt so intense, full of anticipation. President Nisa Farha had sat upright in her grand chair since 6:30, her eyes not leaving the tablet screen displaying again the gloomy data summary about the national judicial condition Anton Prasetya had prepared overnight. Her face looked tired after a long night full of reflection and deep conversation with Reza, but her eyes now radiated sharpness and a steel resolve different from previous days. Despair had turned into resolution. Doubt had vanished, replaced by conviction in a new, immensely important struggle.

The Siti Rahayu case in Sulawesi. The Dito Nugraha case in Kalimantan. Those names kept echoing in her mind, becoming real representation of cold statistical figures about corruption indices, case backlogs, and low public trust. She could no longer delay it. This rule-of-law nation's foundation had to be dismantled and rebuilt from its roots, however great the political risk she had to face.

Right at seven in the morning, one by one her trusted people began entering the room, called by Nisa for a meeting she termed a “Fundamental Strategy Meeting.” First to enter was Anton Prasetya, the Special Staff for Social Affairs whose burden now felt heavier, thin dark circles still visible under his eyes but bringing a new pile of more detailed data and several initial analysis drafts. Followed by Angel Marina, the Palace Communications Head, always alert, ready with a notebook and initial media analysis about how this legal reform issue could potentially be played in public space. Then Dr. Haryati Sulaeman, a senior constitutional law expert from the State Secretariat whose face looked serious but conveyed readiness, her integrity and thoroughness greatly needed by Nisa for navigating this complicated legal matter. Reza Satria, her husband, arrived a few minutes later, this time not merely as businessman or husband, but as Nisa's closest strategic discussion partner, provider of real-world perspective and often the most honest voice of conscience. And last, the figure Nisa awaited most that morning, Professor Budi Santoso, a criminal law academic from a leading university known to be vocal, clean, and brave in criticizing the judicial mafia through his writings in scientific journals and mass media. Nisa specifically invited him, needing reformist out-of-the-box thinking from outside the Palace circle.

After everyone sat around the round meeting table, smaller than the cabinet table, allowing more intense and equal discussion, Nisa opened the meeting without excessive formality. She no longer needed to repeat the details of Siti's or Dito's cases; she knew everyone present had read the brief report she'd shared last night and understood this morning meeting's urgency.

“Good morning, everyone. Thank you for coming this early,” Nisa's voice sounded calm but laden with the weight of the decision she'd made. “We all know why we're gathered here. Quantitative data and qualitative field reports, including several tragic cases we've just learned of together, show a very fundamental and systemic problem in our law enforcement machine.”

She paused briefly, looking at each face before her one by one. “The law we designed with such difficulty in the parliament building to protect the people, turns out it can become blunt, can even turn back into a weapon that oppresses, if its own enforcement machine is fragile, corrupt, and easily intervened.”

“I no longer want us to just make patchwork fixes here and there,” she continued firmly. “Replacing one or two bad actors, fixing one or two procedures. That won't be enough. I want a comprehensive reform, one brave enough to touch the root of the problem, even if it means we have to dismantle an established structure and fight the big powers that have long been comfortable within it.”

She leaned forward slightly. “Today, I want us together, with open minds and courage, to start designing that sword of justice. A sword sharp enough to eradicate the disease of corruption and abuse of authority within the law enforcement body itself, while also being a shield sturdy enough to protect every citizen's rights, especially those weakest and most vulnerable before the law.”

Nisa then gestured to Anton Prasetya to begin the deep-dive data presentation session. Anton stepped forward to the large screen, showing data more detailed than the general statistics he'd shown Nisa yesterday. He highlighted more specific and worrying patterns.

“Our data shows several trends that need all our serious attention, Madam President, everyone,” Anton began his presentation. “First, there's very significant geographic disparity in law enforcement quality. Average case resolution time and indications of judicial corruption practice (based on lawyer and justice-seeker perception surveys) are consistently much higher in courts outside Java Island, especially in regions with minimal budget resources and weak central oversight intensity.”

He moved to the next slide. “Second, from case-type analysis. We found a pattern that land dispute cases involving big corporations or influential local officials, labor dispute cases between workers and big companies, and environmental crime cases like illegal mining or illegal logging, often run very slowly at both investigation and court levels, and not infrequently their verdicts feel odd or don't reflect public sense of justice.” He pointed to a third data point. “Third, there's strong indication of a pattern of non-legal intervention in handling sensitive cases, whether politically or big-business motivated. This is seen from data on sudden transfers of prosecutors or judges handling certain major corruption cases, or informal reports from several credible internal sources about pressure or 'orders' from certain parties to 'secure' a case.”

Anton also highlighted the weak external oversight mechanism. “In regulatory terms, the current Judicial Commission and Prosecutorial Commission have significant limitations regarding independent investigation authority. The sanction recommendations they issue are often non-binding and easily ignored by Supreme Court or Attorney General's Office leadership. On top of that,” Anton added more quietly, “we've also detected a fairly strong internal resistance from certain senior figures within the Supreme Court and Attorney General's Office themselves against external oversight efforts considered 'too meddling' in their household affairs.”

Anton's cold, methodical, data-based presentation further strengthened the situation's urgency in everyone's minds. Dr. Haryati Sulaeman then gave a perspective from formal law and constitutional lens. “Constitutionally and in state administration terms, we indeed have to step very carefully in this judicial reform agenda, Madam President,” said Dr. Haryati with a wisely cautionary tone. “The principle of judicial power independence is the main pillar of our rule-of-law nation whose dignity we must protect. Every reform effort mustn't be interpreted or framed by political opponents as a form of executive power intervention into the judicial domain.”

She continued, “Every plan to revise laws related to the Supreme Court, Prosecutor's Office, Police, even perhaps also the Corruption Eradication Commission and Judicial Commission itself, has to go through a proper legislative process that will certainly be very complicated in Parliament. And it's almost certain, every new legal product will later face a heavy test in the form of judicial review lawsuits at the Constitutional Court.”

“History also records,” Dr. Haryati added, “several judicial reform efforts in previous administration eras often stalled midway, either because of too-strong political resistance, technical implementation problems in the field, or lack of commitment sustainability. Therefore, I agree with Madam President, we need a comprehensive, multi-level approach: regulatory improvement at the law level, strengthening internal and external oversight institutions, fixing internal management at each law enforcement agency, increasing the capacity and integrity of its human resources, and no less important, a long-term effort to build a new legal culture aware of rights and obligations among the wider society.”

Professor Budi Santoso, who'd been listening calmly, nodded in agreement with Dr. Haryati's analysis, then added his critical perspective as an academic who'd long observed judicial practice from 'inside.' “The internal resistance Mr. Anton just mentioned isn't just suspicion, but a very real fact rooted deeply, Madam President,” he said in a calm but piercing voice. “There's a patronage network, alumni ties, a 'corps brotherhood' so solid among certain law enforcement figures, especially those who've long enjoyed the 'comfort zone.' They protect each other. They have a thousand and one ways to 'work over,' hinder the career of, or even remove their own colleagues considered too straight, too idealistic, or trying to expose rot within the institution.”

He looked intently at Nisa. “Forming a special task force like was mentioned earlier might indeed be needed as a spearhead breaker. But that task force has to truly be a 'super body,' have extraordinary investigation and enforcement authority, a clear command structure directly under the President or the new Attorney General, and an extra-strong legal and physical protection mechanism for all its members. Otherwise, I worry that task force will be easily paralyzed or 'get cold feet' midway.”

Professor Budi also highlighted a crucial upstream problem: the law enforcement recruitment system. “The entry point is often already problematic from the start, Madam,” he continued. “Nepotism practices based on family closeness with senior officials, 'placements' from certain political powers, or even suspected money transactions in the selection process for judge or prosecutor candidates are no longer public secrets among legal practitioners. If the seeds entering from the start are already murky because of an unclean selection process, how can we hope the downstream will later be clear and full of integrity?”

Reza Satria then rounded out the discussion by giving a view from the business world and wider society's perspective. “Legal uncertainty due to slow and suspectedly corrupt judiciary has an extraordinarily destructive impact on the business climate, Madam, sir,” he said. “Foreign and domestic investors will think a thousand times before putting long-term capital into Indonesia if they know that even a simple business dispute can take years to be decided, or worse, its verdict can be 'bought' by whoever has more connections or money. He added, “At the SME level, as directly experienced by Ibu Santi in Surabaya the other day, legal injustice or abuse of official authority can immediately kill their business. They feel the law is only sharp downward but blunt upward, only belonging to the rich and powerful.”

However, Reza also saw another side. “But, I also see there's potential collaboration we could explore,” he continued. “Many big companies, including several I know well, now have fairly strong and well-directed CSR programs. Maybe part of that CSR fund could be directed to support these legal reform programs? For example, providing financial support for legal aid institutes so they can expand their free legal aid reach for the poor, providing scholarships for high-achieving law faculty students from underprivileged families so they can later become clean law enforcement officers, or even supporting information technology development to ease public access to legal information and court services.” He looked at Nisa. “We could invite the private sector to become a strategic partner in this struggle, not just a spectator or even part of the problem.”

Angel Marina, who'd been diligently noting the discussion's key points, finally spoke up from a communications standpoint. “Our biggest communication challenge in this legal reform agenda is how to rebuild public trust that's already low, even before the results of this reform can be felt concretely by them,” Angel said. “Political opponents will certainly immediately frame every step of this reform as the President's attempt to control legal institutions for her own political interest, or as merely diverting attention from other economic or social problems.” She looked at Nisa. “We have to be very proactive and strategic in communicating why this reform is urgently needed now. Who benefits most from this reform (namely ordinary people and justice-seekers). And how we'll keep guarding this reform process to stay transparent, accountable, and not abused for momentary interests. Real stories like what happened to Ibu Siti and Mas Dito must keep being raised as the 'face' of this legal reform's urgency.”

That intensive discussion rolled on for almost two full hours. Nisa mostly played the role of active listener, absorbing all perspectives, occasionally throwing sharp questions to test an argument, pushing for deeper thinking and more fundamental solutions. She firmly rejected proposals for mere patchwork or cosmetic solutions. “We can no longer just 'fix' the broken parts,” Nisa asserted amid a heated discussion about strengthening the Judicial Commission. “We must dare to 'rebuild' the foundation of public trust in the law itself. Finally, after fierce debate and mature consideration from various viewpoints, Nisa tapped the oval table gently with the end of her pen, signaling a strategic conclusion beginning to form. Three main pillars of comprehensive legal reform were agreed upon together by that small team:

First Pillar: Internal Clean Sweep. The main focus is cleaning law enforcement institutions from within. Key decision: Drastically strengthening the Judicial Commission (for judge oversight) and Prosecutorial Commission (for prosecutor oversight) through relevant law revision, giving them stronger independent investigation authority and more binding sanction recommendations. The most fundamental is forming the “Judicial Clean Sweep Task Force” (Saber Peradilan Task Force). Its structure will be a cross-institution joint task force (involving the best investigators from the Corruption Eradication Commission, Prosecutor's Office, Police, and analysts from the Financial Transaction Reports and Analysis Center) with strong leadership, independent from its parent institution's structure, and given an extra-strong legal and physical protection mechanism for all its members so they dare act without fear. Additionally, a new, much stricter, more transparent Government Regulation on State Officials' Wealth Reports will soon be drafted, with firm sanctions for law enforcement officers (judges, prosecutors, police) who don't comply or whose wealth is unreasonable.

Second Pillar: Fortress of Independence & Quality. The focus is ensuring judicial independence from external intervention while improving the quality of law enforcement human resources. Key decision: Immediately starting the drafting process for a new Bill on Judicial Office and a new Prosecutorial Service Bill. Both bills' main focus is on totally overhauling the selection, transfer, and promotion mechanisms for law enforcement officers so they're truly transparent, accountable, merit-based (competence and performance), and have a clean integrity track record. An Independent Selection Committee will be formed — whose members consist of credible figures from outside the Supreme Court and Attorney General's Office structure — to select key positions like Supreme Court Justices or Junior Attorneys General. State budget for ethics training programs, legal technical capacity improvement, and continuing education for judges, prosecutors, and police will also be significantly increased.

Third Pillar: Gateway to Justice for All. The focus is expanding and easing access to justice for the public, especially poor and marginalized groups. Key decision: Launching a national “Equal Justice” program covering several main initiatives: total revitalization and expanded service reach of accredited Legal Aid Institutes and Legal Aid Posts at every district court, with a new, more sustainable funding scheme (including exploring the potential of matching funds with private sector CSR funds as Reza proposed). Conducting a People's Court pilot project in several regions to handle simple civil cases (like small debt disputes or simple inheritance) with a far faster, simpler procedure and very cheap or even free cost. And launching a national “Legal Awareness, Dare to Report” campaign that will be commanded by Angel Marina's team, involving public figures, credible social media influencers, and religious leaders to increase public legal awareness and encourage courage to report injustice practices or official extortion without fear.

After the three main reform pillars' framework was agreed upon, Nisa moved to the last, most crucial and politically sensitive issue: who would lead the spearhead of this reform on the front line of prosecution.

“All these big plans, these three pillars, will become a toothless paper tiger if we don't have the right war commander on the front guard of the prosecution institution,” said Nisa, her tone now sounding very serious, looking sharply around the table. “We need a new Attorney General. An Attorney General with no burden of past debt of gratitude. An Attorney General with no affiliation or political debt to any party. An Attorney General who won't be intimidated facing pressure from any power, whether from inside or outside their institution. And most importantly, an Attorney General with the steel nerve to clean their own house from within, even if it means having to prosecute their own friend or senior.”

She paused briefly, letting that ideal but very difficult criteria sink into her team's minds. “I've considered several potential names very carefully over the last few days. Some 'safe' names from within the Prosecutor's Office, some names placed by coalition parties,” she admitted honestly. “But after weighing all the risks and our current situation's urgency, there's only one name that I think truly meets all those fundamental criteria. Even though I'm fully aware, nominating this figure will trigger a political earthquake perhaps far bigger than the Family Bill controversy before.”
Nisa took a deep breath once more, then said it in a firm voice leaving no room for doubt. “I've decided. I'll nominate Ibu Ratna Dewi as Attorney General of the Republic of Indonesia.”

That name hung for a moment in an atmosphere that felt increasingly tense. Professor Budi Santoso nodded slowly first, a thin smile full of appreciation etched on his face. Dr. Haryati Sulaeman looked a little surprised at first, but then gave a small nod, understanding the direction of Nisa's radical but logical thinking. Angel and Anton exchanged a brief glance, their minds immediately working fast mapping the extraordinarily large communication and political implications of this name choice. Reza looked intently at Nisa, a mix of clearly visible worry in his eyes, but also support and admiration for his wife's courage.

“Ratna Dewi?” Dr. Haryati confirmed to clarify, because there were several figures with similar names. “Do you mean the Ratna Dewi who was former Director of Investigation at the Corruption Eradication Commission? Who once caused an uproar because she was 'discarded' from the Commission after handling a major corruption case involving a senior politician? Or the Ratna Dewi who's the critical constitutional law academic from UGM, Madam?”

“The former Director of Investigation at the Corruption Eradication Commission,” Nisa answered firmly, leaving no doubt. “Her integrity reputation needs no doubt, already tested on the hardest anti-corruption battlefield in this country. Her track record is clean of political affiliation. She might be less flexible in practical politics, she might make many parties uncomfortable because of her firmness. But it's exactly that kind of figure we need now to lead the Attorney General's Office. Someone whose main focus is on straight, professional law enforcement, not on small talk or cheap political compromise.”

“Her nomination will almost certainly be flatly rejected by many factions in Parliament, Madam, especially from the opposition and perhaps some of our own coalition,” Dr. Haryati reminded carefully. “They'll certainly consider you're trying to place a 'hardliner' from outside the Prosecutor's Office to pursue certain political targets or to intervene in ongoing cases.”

“The battle at the House Commission III during the fit-and-proper test will certainly be very tough,” Reza added, voicing practical concern. “They'll attack Ibu Ratna from every side, digging for any mistake however small in her past. Is she mentally ready to face that? And are we all here ready to fully back her up?” “We have to be ready,” Nisa replied firmly, looking at Reza then her team in turn. “And I'm sure, after talking with her yesterday, Ibu Ratna Dewi is also ready inside and out. She knows exactly the risks she'll face.” She leaned forward again. “This is no longer about whether it's comfortable or uncomfortable for all of us. This is about saving the Prosecutor's Office institution's dignity and re-establishing the pillar of law in this country. If we want this sword of justice we're designing to truly be sharp and effective, then its hilt must be held by the cleanest, strongest, and bravest hand we can find. And right now, I believe that hand is Ratna Dewi's hand.”

That decision was final. Nisa looked at her team once more. “Anton, immediately prepare Ibu Ratna Dewi's complete profile, anticipate all potential counterattacks and prepare rebuttal data. Angel, design an effective communication strategy to announce and defend this nomination. Focus on her undeniable integrity track record and the urgency of total reform at the Prosecutor's Office. Dr. Haryati, Prof Budi, I need legal and strategic input from you both to convince Parliament and the public of her worthiness.” She then looked at Reza, a thin but meaningful smile on her lips. “And as usual, I most need your support, Mas. To keep my sanity amid the coming storm.”
Reza smiled thinly, returning Nisa's gaze. “Always,” he answered shortly, but heavy with meaning.

That crucial morning meeting ended near nine o'clock. There was a tense aura still lingering, but also a new spirit that felt burning in that room. The Sword of Justice had been designed with three sturdy pillars. And the controversial figure with steel integrity had been chosen to hold it on the front guard.

Nisa Farha stood for a moment before her office's tall window after her whole team had left, gazing at the National Monument standing tall in the distance under Jakarta's bright morning sky. She was fully aware, her decision this morning was an open declaration of war against dark powers — judicial mafia, corrupt politicians, black businessmen — who had long been comfortable playing dirty behind the law's curtain. This battle would drain even greater energy, test patience to its limit, and might demand a sacrifice far greater than she'd ever imagined.

She reached for the intercom handle on her desk, connecting to her personal secretary in the next room. “Mbak Wati,” she said calmly, “please schedule my one-on-one meeting with Ibu Ratna Dewi as soon as possible today or tomorrow morning. It's very important.” She paused briefly. “And also tell Angel, immediately prepare the draft official announcement about the new Attorney General nomination strategy. We won't wait long. Let the real game begin.”

Nisa set down the intercom handle. The scales of justice had tilted too long, too severely. She was resolved, with all existing risk, to start righting them again, restoring the people's trust in their own country's law.

I've long been used to facing pressure like this.” She smiled thinly, the same smile as when she convinced Nisa in their first meeting. “Pressure and threats like this have become my daily breakfast menu back at the KPK, Madam,” she said, a bitter tone of irony in her voice. “My focus now is just one: preparing myself as well as possible in substance to face the fit-and-proper test in Parliament later. Heavy pressure also kept flowing strongly toward Nisa Farha herself. Public discussion about the need for fundamental reform within the Attorney General's Office and Supreme Court body increasingly widened and deepened, no longer just a conversation among legal or political elites alone.

Nisa Farha herself, though choosing not to too often appear commenting directly on the controversy of Ratna Dewi's nomination so as not to seem to intervene in the House process, kept looking for ways to send a support message subtly but strongly to the public. Though she never once mentioned Ratna Dewi's name in her speech, the message and direction of her support for the legal reform agenda to be led by a figure of integrity like Ratna felt so clear and resonated strongly among the academics and law students present.

Finally, after passing through weeks full of tension, intrigue, and that exhausting war of nerves, the fixed schedule for Ratna Dewi's Fit and Proper Test at House Commission III was set: three days away. The capital's air felt increasingly hot, not just because of the arriving dry season, but also because of anticipation ahead of the fiercest political battle about to unfold at the Senayan parliamentary complex.

Piles of preparation materials — her track record data, summary of the Attorney General's Office reform vision and mission she'd compiled together with the Palace team, predicted trick questions from Commission III members along with draft answers — lay on the desk. She already felt intellectually and substantively ready. But she knew, tomorrow's real battle wasn't just a contest of data or legal argument. It would be a mental contest, a test of psychological resilience facing personal attacks, issue-diversion efforts, and perhaps cunning political traps that would be launched by her opponents far more experienced in parliamentary intrigue.

She let out a long sigh, then her gaze unconsciously fell on an old black-and-white photo in a simple frame she always displayed in the corner of her work desk. Her father's photo, a simple prosecutor in a small town in Central Java, who passed away while Ratna was still in law school. Her father was the figure who taught her about the values of honesty and courage in enforcing the law, even though their life was simple and often faced pressure from parties disturbed by her father's straightness of attitude. Remembering her father's calm but principled face seemed to give Ratna new strength that night. She knew exactly, the struggle she'd face tomorrow was a continuation of the struggle her father had once pioneered decades ago. She mustn't waver. Right as she was reflecting, her phone rang softly. President Nisa Farha's name showed on the screen. Ratna took a breath before answering. “Good evening, Madam President,” Ratna greeted calmly.

“Good evening, Ibu Ratna,” Nisa's voice sounded warm and calming on the other end of the line. “I just wanted to call briefly, not wanting to disturb your final preparation. I just wanted to say once again, I fully believe in you.” There was a brief pause. “Tomorrow, face them all with your head held high. Voice the truth you believe in. Answer all their questions with your conscience. Whatever the result later, all Indonesian people longing for justice will see your courage and integrity.”

“Thank you very much for the trust, Madam President,” Ratna Dewi answered, her voice now sounding steadier, the last doubt that might still remain in the corner of her heart seemed to vanish instantly by the injection of spirit from the President. “I'm ready.”

After ending the call, Ratna Dewi stood, walked toward her apartment window, gazing at the twinkling lights of Jakarta city below. The war of nerves might have reached its peak. Intimidation might continue. But tonight, she felt more ready than ever. Ready to enter the real battle arena at House Commission III tomorrow. Ready to fight for her conviction in clean and just law, for her father, for President Nisa, and for all Indonesian people longing for change. The show was about to begin.
