Ratna Dewi directly appointed a select Public Prosecutor (JPU) team consisting of young prosecutors with integrity and courage to handle this case, ensuring no intervention or 'case-securing' attempts from within. The case development from High Court Judge AS's sting operation ran fast. In the following months, the Task Force again made several important arrests that further shook the judicial world: a senior prosecutor at the High Prosecutor's Office suspected of acting as a case broker for several big land cases, and a top-tier lawyer long known as 'slippery' and suspected of often being an intermediary for bribes between his corporate clients and rogue judges or prosecutors. This string of arrests sent a very strong signal throughout the country that the era of impunity for legal mafia would truly soon end.

Of course, counterattack from parties feeling disturbed by Ratna Dewi and the Saber Peradilan Task Force's breakthroughs was no less fierce. The sting operation suspects — High Court Judge AS, the senior prosecutor, the top-tier lawyer — hired the best and most expensive legal teams to fight in court. They filed pretrial motions, questioning the validity of evidence used by the Task Force, trying to build public opinion that they were victims of criminalization or unhealthy competition between law enforcement agencies. Media affiliated with the political opposition network continuously 'fried' the issue of 'procedural flaws' in the Task Force's operation, framing Ratna Dewi as a repressive, power-hungry Attorney General figure, and creating a narrative as if a 'star wars' was occurring between institutions (KPK vs Prosecutor's Office vs Police) that only harmed national stability.

In Parliament, Pak Hardiman and friends again used their oversight function to pressure. They held a sudden Hearing Meeting (RDP) with Attorney General Ratna Dewi and the Saber Peradilan Task Force leadership, grilling them with cornering questions about the Task Force's work methods, questioning the legal basis for the Task Force's formation, even trying to hinder budget allocation for the Attorney General's Office reform program.

However, amid all that pressure and counterattack, President Nisa Farha stood firm as the main political 'shield' for Ratna Dewi and her legal reform agenda. In every opportunity to speak before the public — whether in official press conferences, state speeches, or exclusive interviews — Nisa consistently gave full and unwavering support to Attorney General Ratna Dewi and the Saber Peradilan Task Force's hard work. She reaffirmed her government's commitment to eradicate judicial mafia to its roots, asked all parties to respect the ongoing legal process, and reminded that legal reform was a constitutional mandate that must be carried out without compromise for the benefit of all Indonesian people. Behind the scenes, Nisa also kept intensively lobbying coalition party leaders not to waver under political pressure and to keep supporting Ratna Dewi in parliament.

The Palace's communication team under Angel Marina's command also worked tirelessly to manage the public narrative. They proactively released detailed data and facts about cases being handled by the Saber Peradilan Task Force to counter misleading information spread by the opposing side. They continuously re-echoed real stories about how this legal reform began giving positive impact to ordinary people's justice, like the story of the grandmother in Central Java who finally won her land dispute, or the story of the traditional village in Sumatra that succeeded in stopping illegal mining thanks to their report being seriously followed up by new, clean District Prosecutor's Office officials. The message meant to be conveyed was clear: this legal reform wasn't just an elite political battle in Jakarta, but truly concerned the fate and justice of all Indonesian people.

That first wave of cleaning within the Attorney General's Office and other judicial institutions indeed caused great turbulence. Polarization within the Adhyaksa corps sharpened between the pro-reform camp now feeling a fresh wind, the status quo camp continuing open and covert counterattack, and the majority camp choosing to 'lay low' while waiting to see which way the wind would favor. Ratna Dewi kept working hard day and night, leading by example of integrity and firmness of professionalism, trying to navigate that internal battlefield full of mines. And Nisa Farha kept standing firm giving full political support from the Palace. Slowly but surely, the scales of justice that had long tilted severely began moving, seeking a new, straighter balance point.
A Year Later (Mid-Year 2049)

That hard work, firmness of principle, and courage to swim against the current finally began bearing real fruit whose impact could be widely felt by society. Almost a year after Ratna Dewi was inaugurated Attorney General and comprehensive legal reform began rolling systematically, Indonesia's law enforcement landscape began showing signs of change for the better. That fruit of justice tasted so sweet for those long marginalized. Siti Rahayu, the brave girl from Central Sulawesi, after going through a long and exhausting continued legal struggle up to the Case Review (PK) level at the Supreme Court (whose panel was now partly filled by new supreme court justices from a cleaner independent selection), finally succeeded in winning back rights to her family's inherited land once unjustly seized by a corrupt village head years ago. With help from an education scholarship from a CSR program of one of Reza Satria Group's partner companies and local community support inspired by her tenacity, Siti was now in her final semester at the Teacher Training and Education Faculty of a local university in Palu, one step closer to realizing her dream of becoming an elementary school teacher who would teach values of honesty and courage to her students. Her story became an inspiring symbol of how law siding with truth could become a path of liberation for the weak.

In West Kalimantan, Dito Nugraha, the idealistic young journalist and “Bold Spark” alumnus, also finally could breathe the air of freedom and justice. After going through a fairer and more professional appeal process at the High Court (whose judges were also relatively cleaner of local power intervention post-reform wave), he was declared not guilty and freed from all defamation charges under the Electronic Information Law that had entangled him. That appeal verdict explicitly stated that his investigative journalism work about alleged illegal mining extortion had met journalistic code of ethics standards and was protected by the Press Law. This verdict became an important jurisprudence giving stronger legal protection for press freedom and citizen journalism in regions prone to intimidation. Dito himself was now one of the most respected young investigative journalists in Kalimantan, his writing on his personal blog (now far more professional) often becoming a national media reference, and he'd just received a prestigious award from an independent institution for his courage in uncovering an environmental corruption case. Similar stories, though maybe not all covered nationally by media, emerged from various corners of the country. A traditional fishing community group on Java's northern coast finally won their collective lawsuit at the State Administrative Court (PTUN) against an illegal sea sand mining permit that destroyed the marine ecosystem and their livelihood source. Hundreds of victims of illegal online loans (pinjol) once trapped in suffocating debt and terrorized by rude debt collectors, now began getting more real legal protection and access to debt restructuring assistance through the Investment Alert Task Force working more effectively thanks to better inter-agency coordination. A Sumba ikat weaving craftswoman whose work was once pirated by a big designer without permission, finally succeeded in winning an Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) dispute at the Commercial Court after getting pro bono legal assistance from an LBH now more active in reaching creative economy actors in the regions.

That positive change was also reflected concretely in macro statistical figures. Indonesia's Corruption Perception Index (CPI) released by Transparency International showed an encouraging rise in the past year, an early signal that Indonesia was starting to move out of the group of countries with corruption levels considered serious. Justice-seeker satisfaction surveys conducted periodically by the Supreme Court and independent survey institutions also showed a drastic increase in public satisfaction levels with district court services (especially in process speed, cost transparency, and ease of information access) and with the quality of free legal aid services from LBH/Posbakum. Case backlogs at the Supreme Court began decreasing, cut by almost 20 percent thanks to improved case management and increased number of quality supreme court justices. And no less important, Indonesia's investment climate felt increasingly conducive. Foreign investment (PMA) and domestic investment (PMDN) flows recorded stable positive growth, partly driven by increased perception of legal certainty and reduced extortion practice or judicial corruption that had long been a bogeyman for the business world. That fundamental legal reform truly gave a broad positive impact on all aspects of the nation's life.

The echo of Indonesia's legal reform success, once perhaps unimaginable, began being heard as far as Southeast Asia. Regional media like The Straits Times and Channel News Asia, and several policy study institutions in Manila and Kuala Lumpur, began positively highlighting the initial progress Indonesia achieved in improving its legal and judicial governance. Indonesia, once often looked down upon regarding law enforcement in the region, now slowly began to be cited as an example worth noting by neighboring countries, an early sign that strong political will from top leadership, supported by the courage of an integrity-driven law enforcement figure and active civil society participation, could begin moving change even in a system already considered chronically corrupt.

That good news came on a bright morning in mid-2049. An official letter with ASEAN Secretariat letterhead, sent from its representative office in Jakarta, arrived on President Nisa Farha's desk. That letter contained an honorary invitation: inviting the President of the Republic of Indonesia, Ibu Nisa Farha, to become keynote speaker at the ASEAN Law Ministers' Meeting on Anti-Corruption to be held in Manila in a few weeks. Indonesia, through President Nisa, was specifically asked to share its initial experience and steps taken in carrying out legal and judicial reform, considered promising for neighboring countries struggling against similar problems. Nisa read that invitation letter repeatedly, her heart trembling holding back emotion. This wasn't just formal recognition on paper. This was an honor for the Indonesian nation. Proof that the hard work and risk-filled struggle she and her whole team had done over the past year — from inaugurating Ratna Dewi, to uncovering the High Court Judge AS sting operation case — was beginning to catch the region's attention. Neighboring countries began recognizing Indonesia as an example worth noting in building rule of law. She accepted that invitation with deep gratitude, but also with awareness of the great responsibility accompanying it to be able to deliver the right and honest message at that regional forum later.

As the Manila meeting schedule drew closer, Indonesia began receiving comparative study visits from several Southeast Asian neighboring countries — the Philippines, Vietnam, and Malaysia — interested in directly studying Indonesia's style of legal reform model. They wanted to know in more detail how the Saber Peradilan Task Force worked effectively uncovering legal mafia, how the independent and merit-based judge and prosecutor selection mechanism was run, how the LBH funding scheme involving the private sector could succeed, or how the government balanced Electronic Information Law enforcement with protecting freedom of expression post-Dito Nugraha case. Indonesia, once often lectured by neighboring countries about good governance, now slowly began being viewed as an early example worth studying in the region. Regional media coverage of Indonesia also began shifting, from once often highlighting corruption cases, now also beginning to be colored by positive news about legal reform steps and promising economic potential.

However, amid all that euphoria of world recognition and proud progress data, Nisa Farha kept trying to keep her feet firmly planted on the ground. She was fully aware that the homework to realize true rule of law in this country was still very much unfinished. Latent resistance from status quo groups feeling their interests disturbed by this reform certainly still existed, though maybe now moving more quietly and waiting for a chance to rise again. The culture of corruption, collusion, and nepotism rooted for decades in part of the bureaucracy and law enforcement officers couldn't possibly disappear totally in just a year. Maintaining judicial institution independence from future political or business intervention would also be an ongoing challenge requiring tight oversight and unceasing commitment from all parties.

In internal evaluation meetings with her team, Nisa instead emphasized more the importance of not being complacent by praise and international recognition. “Consider all this a bonus, an encouragement,” she told Anton, Angel, Ratna Dewi (who occasionally joined meetings via video conference), and related ministers. “Our main focus must remain on internal consolidation, on continuous improvement in the field, on ensuring that this 'fruit of justice' we're beginning to harvest can truly be enjoyed equally by all levels of society, down to the farthest village corners, not just becoming a success story in the capital or at international forums.” She also began thinking about the next steps: how to integrate this legal reform success with reform agendas in other interrelated sectors, like public service bureaucracy reform, strengthening legal and ethics education from an early age, and more holistic anti-corruption eradication across all levels of government.

The night before her departure to Manila to deliver her speech at that ASEAN forum, Nisa again stood on the Palace balcony with Reza, gazing at the twinkling lights of Jakarta stretching like a carpet under the clear night sky.

“It still feels like a dream, Mas,” Nisa said quietly, her head resting comfortably on Reza's shoulder. “Seeing Indonesia, our country once often looked down upon in law enforcement matters, now instead invited as keynote speaker at an ASEAN legal forum. Before, we were always the ones lectured by neighboring countries about how to eradicate corruption.”

Reza smiled gently, holding his wife's shoulder tighter. “That's not a dream, Nisa,” he answered quietly but with full conviction. “That's the real result of your tireless hard work for almost a decade. That's the fruit of your courage to take the biggest political risk in your life for your conviction in justice. That's the fruit of your steadfastness on principle when everyone tried to pull you toward compromise.” He looked intently into Nisa's eyes. “You, Ibu Ratna Dewi, Anton, Angel, Professor Budi, and all the good people who still believe in change in this country, you've all succeeded in turning things around. You've proven that fundamental reform is possible, even in a system already considered the most corrupt.” Reza paused briefly, a proud smile on his lips. “And our neighboring countries are beginning to recognize it.”

Nisa returned Reza's smile, her heart filled with overflowing gratitude. Yes, the region was beginning to recognize it. Indonesia, under her leadership, had at least won a fundamental and immensely important battle against itself, against the chronic disease of judicial corruption that had long damaged the nation's foundations. That fruit of justice was beginning to taste sweet, not only for Siti Rahayu in Sulawesi or Dito Nugraha in Kalimantan, but for the whole nation's hope for a better legal future. And the light of justice from the Nusantara land now began shining dimly but surely, illuminating a glimmer of hope in the Southeast Asian region.

Nisa Farha's journey as President of the Republic of Indonesia, which began with the embers of concern over her family's fate, continued with a spark of courage to ignite the nation's creative potential, and culminated in a big gamble to straighten the country's scales of justice again, might not yet be fully complete. Much homework still awaited. But at least tonight, under Jakarta's starry sky, she could feel that this nation's compass direction now pointed more firmly toward the noble ideal of true rule of law. And she was ready to continue that journey, with a wiser heart, a stronger soul, and love for the country that never waned. The light after that series of storms now felt not just warmly calming, but also became a torch illuminating the long road ahead of them.
